articles.body_html:
A Little Room to Breathe

I was polishing a few coffee cups behind the counter when the bell above the door rang.

A regular walked in, his jacket draped over one arm. His phone kept lighting up every few moments.

He took his usual seat by the window and placed the phone on the table. The screen lit up again. He glanced at it, sighed, and finally turned it face down.

I looked at him and smiled.

"Let's get you something different today."

He looked up.

"No double espresso today?"

"Today, I'm making you a cup of The Pause."

He looked at me.

"That sounds less like coffee and more like advice."

I laughed.

"Decaf flat white. A little gentler, with smooth, velvety milk. Something to take your time with."

He smiled.

"All right. I'll trust you today."

I turned to prepare it.

The decaf espresso slowly flowed into a warm ceramic cup. I steamed the milk until it was silky and smooth, then poured it slowly, leaving a thin layer of foam on top.

One cup of The Pause, ready.

I placed it in front of him.

"Busy lately?"

"All day."

"Get everything done?"

He glanced at his phone.

"Not even close. There's still a pile of things waiting."

"Then how did you find time to come here?"

He smiled.

"That's the problem. I'm sitting here, but my mind is still running through everything I haven't finished."

I pointed at his phone.

"Doesn't look like it's planning to leave you alone, either."

"Haha. Pretty much."

He picked up The Pause and took a sip.

"Sometimes even when I'm resting, I feel like I should be doing something. Learning something new, finishing a plan, or at least checking my email."

I looked at him.

"Sounds like your system never enters idle mode."

He laughed.

"You know your stuff."

"Used to make a living doing it."

"You worked in IT?"

"Software testing, mostly. I also managed a test team. Back then, whenever my phone rang, I'd check whether something had gone wrong in production, whether another release had a bug, or whether the CI pipeline had turned red again."

He laughed.

"Then I guess we're in the same line of work."

"More or less. These days, my main test subject is the coffee machine."

We both laughed.

I put the clean cups back on the shelf and said casually,

"Today might be a good day for a story."

"What kind of story?"

I took an old book from the shelf beside the counter.

"One written by an ancient Chinese thinker."

The Great Bird and the Little One

He looked at the cover.

"Zhuangzi?"

"Heard of him?"

"Only the name. Never read him."

"That's fine. His stories don't require much background to understand."

I opened the book.

"This one is called Free and Easy Wandering."

He repeated the title.

"Free and Easy Wandering? Sounds like a travel guide."

I laughed.

"If it were, I hope you'd find it useful today."

Then I told him a story.

Long ago, a Chinese thinker named Zhuangzi wrote about an enormous fish.

It lived in the northern sea and was called Kun. It was so huge that no one knew how many thousands of miles it stretched.

One day, Kun transformed into a bird called Peng.

Its back was just as enormous. When it spread its wings, they seemed to cover the whole sky.

The bird was preparing to fly south, toward a distant sea.

It wasn't an easy journey.

It needed a powerful wind to lift it. Only then could it rise through the air, climbing to a height of ninety thousand miles before heading south.

I paused for a moment and took a sip of water.

"Here's where the story gets interesting."

He looked at me.

"What happens next?"

"There's a cicada and a little dove in a tree. They see the great bird flying so high and can't make sense of it."

They might have thought something like this:

We take off from the ground and fly as far as the trees nearby. Sometimes we don't even make it that far and end up back on the ground. No big deal.

Why would anyone need to fly ninety thousand miles into the sky and travel all the way to the southern sea?

He laughed.

"So the little bird thinks the great bird is being a bit dramatic?"

"Something like that."

"Then which one does Zhuangzi think is right?"

I kept a finger between the pages and thought for a moment.

"I'm not sure how he'd answer that. But I don't think we have to pick a winner every time we read this story."

He looked at me.

"What do you mean?"

"Well, the great bird has somewhere to go. The little one has its familiar branches. They fly differently, so naturally they live different lives."

I pointed toward the window.

"If that little bird spent every day watching the great bird in the sky, it might forget to enjoy the branch it's sitting on."

He smiled but didn't say anything.

After a moment, he spoke.

"Sometimes I feel that way when I see other people getting promoted, starting businesses, or landing better jobs."

"Envious?"

"A little. Mostly, I start wondering whether I should be doing something more with my own life."

He looked down at his cup.

"It feels like everyone is running forward. If you stop, you'll get left behind."

I didn't answer right away.

Outside, a small bird landed on a branch. It stayed there for a moment, then flew away.

"Someone else's ninety thousand miles doesn't have to be your destination."

He looked up at me.

"That's a good line for a coffee shop."

"Then let's leave it here for now."

He smiled.

After a while, he seemed to remember something.

"This actually reminds me of a project we're working on."

"What happened?"

"It's an internal tool that was originally built for a few dozen people. Now, during the architecture review, everyone's already discussing how to scale it to millions of users. Microservices, caching, auto-scaling... the whole package."

"Do you have millions of users now?"

"Dozens."

I laughed.

"Are those few dozen people happy with it?"

"Yeah. Actually, it's been working just fine."

"Is something wrong with it?"

He thought for a moment.

"Not really."

"So when are you expecting those millions of users to show up?"

He shrugged.

"No one knows. Everyone just thinks we should be ready."

I nodded.

"There's nothing wrong with thinking ahead. But you can still start by doing a good job for the few dozen people who are actually using it."

He laughed.

"If I said that in our architecture review, we'd probably have an argument."

"Then I'll keep saying it here."

He picked up his cup and took another sip.

"At least no one here is asking me to draw an architecture diagram."

"Not without ordering coffee first."

A Tree That Wasn't Good for Anything

I turned to another page.

"Zhuangzi also told a story about a tree. It's one of my favorites."

In the story, Zhuangzi's friend Huizi mentioned a very unusual tree.

Its trunk was thick but twisted and uneven. A carpenter couldn't cut a straight, usable piece of timber from it. Its branches bent in all sorts of directions, making them unsuitable for building anything.

When carpenters passed by, they barely gave it a glance.

Huizi thought the tree was completely useless.

But Zhuangzi asked: why not plant it in a wide-open field?

You could walk around it whenever you liked.

And when you were tired, you could lie down in its shade.

Because the tree didn't meet a carpenter's standards, no one would come along with an axe to cut it down.

He looked out the window.

"So it survived because it was useless?"

"That's one way to put it."

I looked outside too.

"But it made me think of something else."

"What's that?"

"Think about the trees in a forest that grow straight and tall. Their trunks make good timber, so people value them. Sooner or later, someone comes along with an axe."

I picked up my cup and took a sip.

"Meanwhile, the crooked ones aren't going to become beams or furniture. Nobody has much use for them. So they just keep growing where they are."

He smiled.

"Sounds like not being good enough can sometimes be lucky."

"Maybe."

I looked out the window.

"But I doubt that tree ever worried about any of that."

He followed my gaze.

"It just keeps growing?"

"Something like that."

He was quiet for a moment.

"I suppose there's a bit of a lesson for software development in there, too."

"How so?"

"We're always trying to refactor old code. Improve performance, clean up the architecture, make things more reusable. Sometimes a little tool works perfectly well, but someone decides it's not elegant enough and needs to be redesigned."

"Of course, bugs need fixing. Code needs maintenance."

I put down my cup.

"But some things are fine just doing the job they were made for."

He laughed.

"That doesn't sound like something a former test manager would say."

"Then you probably don't know how often I used to ask developers to change their code."

He burst out laughing.

After a while, he looked at me.

"So how did you end up leaving IT?"

I didn't answer immediately.

I put the cup back on the counter and thought for a moment.

"Then the AI wave came. The company reorganized, and my role was cut."

He looked surprised.

"You were laid off?"

"Yeah."

"That must have been rough."

"It was. At first, I didn't know what to do with myself."

I wiped down the counter.

"I used to spend every day looking at releases, bugs, test coverage, and delivery schedules. Whenever my phone rang, I assumed there was something waiting for me to deal with."

"And then?"

"For a while, my phone got a lot quieter."

I smiled.

"That took some getting used to. I was so accustomed to having a list of things to do every day that when the list disappeared, I didn't quite know what to do with myself."

He said nothing.

"Sometimes I'd still open my laptop to see what was new in the industry and what other people were building, as if I'd fall behind if I didn't."

I paused.

"Eventually, I did that less and less."

"And then you opened this place?"

"Yeah. I started learning how to make coffee, and eventually rented this space. I didn't realize how many things there were to deal with when you open a coffee shop."

He laughed.

"Doesn't sound much less busy."

"Not really. The coffee machine breaks, the beans need ordering, and the bills still have to be paid at the end of the month."

We both laughed.

I picked up a cup and checked its rim.

"Still, the things I spend my days on are a little different now."

He looked at me but didn't ask anything more.

You Don't Have to Fly That High Today

A little later, his phone lit up again.

He glanced at it, picked it up, then finally put it back on the table.

"Honestly, sometimes I feel like I just can't switch off."

"Work?"

"Not just work. It feels like I have to do something every day. Learn something new, finish some plan, keep improving. Even when I'm resting, I feel like I should be reading a book or listening to a course."

I smiled.

"Well, you've spent a little time with Zhuangzi today."

He looked at me.

"So this counts as a learning task?"

"No. You just listened to me tell two stories."

He laughed.

I put down the cup in my hand.

"Sometimes it's fine to do nothing for a while."

He looked at me.

"You're busy running this place every day, aren't you?"

"Of course. Grinding beans, wiping tables, washing cups, remembering how everyone likes their coffee."

"So how do you manage not to rush around all the time?"

I thought for a moment.

"Not always. Sometimes I mess up a coffee, keep someone waiting, or have too many things piling up. It gets frustrating."

I pointed at the cup in his hands.

"But when you're having a coffee, you can at least finish it before moving on to the next thing."

He smiled.

I went back behind the counter and made myself an Americano.

Then I took my cup and sat at another table by the window.

He looked at me.

"You're not busy now?"

"Not right now."

We both laughed.

Outside, the leaves moved gently in the breeze.

Inside the café, the only sounds were the occasional hum of the coffee machine and the soft clink of cups against wooden tables.

Neither of us said anything.

Neither of us was in a hurry to do anything.

One Cup of The Pause

His phone lit up once more.

He glanced at it but didn't reply right away. Then he put it back on the table.

"I don't think I've done anything useful today."

I looked at the nearly empty cup of The Pause in front of him.

"Didn't you just finish a decaf flat white?"

"Does that count?"

"Well, at least The Pause wasn't wasted."

He laughed.

"You know, I haven't sat like this in a very long time."

"Then stay a little longer."

After a while, he put his phone in his pocket and stood up.

"I should get going. Still have a few things to take care of."

"Take it easy. See you tomorrow."

He straightened his jacket and glanced out the window one last time.

"Maybe the little bird has an easier life than the great bird."

I smiled.

"Maybe. Who knows?"

He walked out, and the bell above the door rang.

I returned to the counter and picked up his empty cup.

Outside, the tree was still there.

Its trunk wasn't straight, and its branches weren't particularly impressive. When the wind passed through, they swayed gently, then settled back into place.

I picked up my Americano and looked out the window.

Nothing particularly special had happened today.

And that was just fine.

Some afternoons, you don't have to fly ninety thousand miles.

Sometimes, it's enough to sit down, take your time, and finish a cup of coffee you really enjoy.

articles.title: Lazy Senior Dev Mode Made My App Smaller. Was It Better?
articles.description: Raise your hand if you've been curious about Ponytail. 🙋 Same spec, same model, same prompt. One...
articles.body_html:
Raise your hand if you've been curious about Ponytail. 🙋 Same spec, same model, same prompt. One build with the rules off, one with them on.

TL;DR: I'd been using Ponytail's principles in my builds and got curious what they really change. So I rebuilt one of my summer apps twice with Claude Code, once with the Ponytail ruleset off and once with it on, and compared both against my original. Ponytail's build came out smaller, a little cheaper, and the only one with no must-fix bugs, though how much smaller depends on how you measure. Whether that made it the better app is a different question.

I had three copies of the same app open in three tabs, and I liked the biggest one best.

All three did the same thing. The app is called Spell It: you type a word, and it builds that word out of periodic table symbols. Type banana and you get Ba · Na · Na, which is barium, sodium, sodium. A fruit, spelled entirely in chemistry. The fun part is typing your own name to see if you're made of elements too. One was the version I shipped last summer. The other two were built that morning by Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent, from the same spec. One of those had a ruleset called Ponytail switched on. The other didn't.

The Ponytail build was the smallest. It passed every check. When an auditor went through all three, it was the only one with no must-fix problems. And it was the one I'd least want to show someone.

earlgreyhot1701D / ponytail-spell-it

Same PRD, built with and without the Ponytail ruleset, compared against my original

Ponytail x Spell It

Same PRD. Same model. Same prompt. One build with the Ponytail ruleset off, one with it on, both compared against the version I made last summer.

Short version: Ponytail made the app smaller (half the lines, about a quarter less by file size), a little cheaper and faster, with no must-fix bugs. It also took out the parts I liked.

Read the full write-up on dev.to.

The experiment is frozen as it ran on Nov 21, 2026 (tag experiment-2026-11-21). Anything added later is listed in ADDENDUM.md.

The problem

AI coding agents tend to build more than you asked for. Extra abstractions, extra files, a library where the browser already has the feature. The code works, but it's bigger than it needs to be, and bigger code is harder to read, review, and trust.

Ponytail is an open source ruleset that tries to fix…

View on GitHub

Lazy, on purpose

Ponytail is an open source ruleset by Dietrich Gebert that you install into a coding agent. Its pitch is that AI agents over-build: extra files, extra abstractions, a library where the browser already has the feature. Ponytail tells the agent to act like the laziest senior dev in the room and climb a ladder before writing anything. Does this need to exist? Is it already in the codebase? Does the standard library handle it? Does the browser? Can it be one line? Only then, the minimum code that works, plus one small test if the logic is tricky.

The repo's own benchmark reports about 53% less code, 41% less time, and 26% lower cost than the same agent without it.

I wasn't new to it. I'd been using Ponytail's principles in my own builds, not the plugin. In Dead Keys, my typing game for the Kiroween hackathon, Ponytail's rules file rode along unchanged as a steering file for Kiro, AWS's AI coding tool. A steering file is a set of instructions the agent reads on every task. What I'd never done was check what those rules changed. Every app I'd built with them, I'd only ever seen one way. So this one was just to see: same app, rules off, rules on, side by side.

One spec, three builds

I picked Spell It, one of the small apps I built every day in July for Netlify's Hot AR Summer 2026. It's tiny, but it has real logic: finding the spelling that fits the most letters is a little search problem, so Ponytail's "add a test" rule had something to bite on. It also has plenty of room to over-build, and it already had a finished design to compare against.

Claude (Opus 5.5, in chat) read my original and wrote a PRD from it: a one-page spec of what the app must do. Every feature got a label. MUST means build it. STUB means leave a comment for later, don't build it. NEVER means no storage, no network calls, no AI calls. The PRD also had nine acceptance checks, tests the finished app had to pass, plus the original's colors and fonts, and nothing about how to write the code.

Then the setup, kept as boring as possible:

Original A B
Built Last summer Claude Code Claude Code
Model n/a Opus 5.5 Opus 5.5
Ponytail n/a Off Full
Got n/a The PRD and one prompt The PRD and one prompt

Each build ran in a fresh session, in an empty folder holding only the PRD, with no personal rules files. Ponytail was installed for both. For A, I switched it off with its own off command before sending anything. Both got the exact same prompt:

Build the app described in PRD.md. Put it in one index.html in this folder. When you're done, tell me how to check it against the acceptance checks.

My job was to stay out of the way. I'd planned one-line follow-ups for any failed check. Neither build needed one.

Here's the same demo on all three: type banana, click periodic, type jazz.

Original (my summer 2026 version)

Build A (Claude Code, Ponytail off)

Build B (Claude Code, Ponytail full)

Half the lines. Not half the code.

Here's what came back. JavaScript is the logic. CSS is the look.

Original A: off B: full
JavaScript lines 319 151 109
CSS lines 595 227 61
Total lines 989 416 206
File size 28.9 KB 14.1 KB 10.8 KB
Acceptance checks 9 of 9 8 of 9 9 of 9
Build cost n/a $0.85 $0.73
Build time n/a 1m 49s 1m 29s

By lines, B is half the size of A. By file size, it's about a quarter smaller. The gap is real, but part of it is formatting: B packs more onto each line. All 118 elements fit on about 12 lines in B. My original spreads them over 40.

Ponytail also saved a little time and money, but not much:

A: off B: full Saved
Build time 1m 49s 1m 29s 20 seconds
Build cost $0.85 $0.73 12 cents

Why so little? I picked a tiny app on purpose, so the builds were small to begin with, and there wasn't much to save. Every session also costs something just to get started. In one of my audit sessions, turning Ponytail on cost $0.30 before it did any work at all. On a bigger app, the savings would have more room to show up.

Both builds also wrote self-checks, small tests that run the acceptance table every time the page loads. Counting console.assert lines, A has 7 and B has 8. My original has none.

The number that surprised me was A. Plain Claude Code, no Ponytail, came in under half the size of my original. The PRD did a lot of that work before Ponytail ever showed up. When every feature is labeled MUST, STUB or NEVER, there isn't much left to over-build.

The cut came from the look

Look at the CSS row again. B has about a tenth of my original's styling by lines, and about a quarter by file size. Either way, most of it is gone.

That's where the background texture went, and the brass frame with the little screws in the corners, and the big title. Ponytail treats those as things nobody asked for.

And here's the part that's on me: nobody did ask. My PRD listed the colors, the fonts and a thin brass frame. It never mentioned the texture or the screws. Ponytail builds what the spec says, so design that isn't written down disappears. For a utility, that's fair. For a toy, the pizzazz is the point, and next time it goes in the spec.

I gave each build a gut score, one to five, for "would I ship it as is":

Original A: off B: full
5 4 4

A and B are one-shots. They'd get there with a few UI tweaks. They just didn't start there.

The bug went to the build without Ponytail

The one acceptance check that failed was mine to design and A's to miss: paste in a very long word and the page shouldn't freeze. I tested with 10,200 letters.

Time per keystroke
Original 0.03 seconds
A: off 1.1 to 1.8 seconds
B: full about 0.3 seconds

I hadn't set a number for "freeze" before testing. Afterward, I drew the line at one second per keystroke. The gap was wide enough that any line between half a second and a second gives the same answer.

A froze. When it finished building, A had told me a 10,200-letter word "shows results right away." Later, A's own review admitted it had only checked that the word worked, not how fast, and called its earlier claim wrong.

The fix the review suggested was one attribute: cap how many letters the input box takes. My original has done that since July, with an 80-letter limit. Summer me had already solved a bug that a brand-new build shipped.

Fewer lines isn't the score

If you've been building for a while, you might be squinting at that first table. Fewer lines isn't the same as better software. I agree, and this test shows it. Even the line count was misleading.

My original is the longest of the three, and it's the one I'd ship. Most of its extra lines are the background, the frame, and the big title, the parts a person notices. Build B is the smallest, and some of its lines are self-tests my original never had. The one real bug had nothing to do with size; the fix is a single attribute.

I think line count measures what you have to read and maintain. It doesn't measure whether the software is right, fast, accessible, or fun. Ponytail is good at cutting that first cost. The rest is still on me.

The judge needed checking too

Ponytail ships with an audit command that reviews a whole project and ranks what to fix. I ran it on all three.

Original A: off B: full
Must-fix 1 1 0
Should-fix 4 1 2
Nice to have 2 3 3

It found real things. My original still had a placeholder where the social share image should be. All three builds made screen readers read the whole result aloud on every keystroke, which is a gap in my PRD, not in any builder.

It also made things up. It called my sign-off line, "Powered by NLP," a false claim about the code. It described Spell It as a college-affiliated project, which it isn't. And it suggested a test where banana spells as B · A · Na · Na. A isn't an element. That test would fail.

So the audit earned its place, with the same rule I use for everything else: check it against the file.

Who did what

This was a three-way build, like most of mine.

  • Claude Code (Opus 5.5) built A and B from the PRD, in two separate sessions on my computer.
  • Claude (Opus 5.5, in chat) wrote the PRD from my original, ran every acceptance check in an automated browser, timed the long-word freeze, made the GIFs, and caught that it had under-tested the long word the first time.
  • Ponytail ran the reviews and audits.
  • I picked the app, set the rules for a fair test, stayed off the keyboard during the builds, checked the auditor's claims, and scored what I'd ship.

What it can't tell you

  • One small app, one run per build. It's a case study, not a benchmark, and AI builds vary from run to run.
  • Ponytail was installed but switched off for A, not uninstalled.
  • The PRD was written from my original, so the original had a head start on matching it.
  • A and B were audited in the same session that built them. The original got a fresh session.
  • Nobody tested it with a real screen reader or on a real phone.

Try it

Everything is in the repo: the PRD, all three builds, the full scorecard, and the raw audit output. Every build is one HTML file. Download it, double-click it, and type your name.

The repo is frozen as the experiment ran, under a tag. Anything I added later, including scripts that rerun the size, check, and timing numbers in this post, and the screenshots behind the costs, is listed in its addendum.

If you want to repeat the test, the README has the steps. It cost me $2.95 across all three sessions, audits included.

I came in expecting a number. I left with a question I'd like other builders' takes on: when an agent makes your code smaller, how do you tell whether it cut fat or cut flavor?

Mostly by playing with it.

This is my first post as a member of Necoz, a community that builds small, simple, useful tools. Fitting, for a post about small, simple code. Thanks for having me. 🐱

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect. That is the lens I am writing from.

Built and tested with AI assistance in November 2026. Ponytail's benchmark numbers come from its README. These tools move fast, so check the source before you quote me.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

articles.title: I Know It's You, But I Can't Prove It

articles.body_html:
Imagine you have a list of usernames and passwords. Then a user logs in to your web application. You check and verify that they are indeed on the list. So you let them in. Case solved, yes?

Not quite.

Logging in is only the beginning. What happens when they try editing their profile, posting a comment, or retrieving data they own? Of course, they should have access to it because it's theirs. But we can't blindly trust every request just because we verified them once.

You know it's them, but how can you prove it?

Well, what if we could pop the login form every single time they do something?

NO.

That would be a nightmare for the user experience. Just imagine this scenario:

Frustrating, isn't it? Nobody wants to prove their identity every time they do something. It's like having to solve a CAPTCHA over and over just to prove you're not a bot.

Thankfully, there's a better way. This is where JWT comes in.

What The Heck is a JWT?

This is literally my reaction when I first read about the term when building my Kanban backend. But it's actually quite simple.

A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a signed token that a server can issue to a client after successfully authenticating a user. I know it's a lot of terms but we can think of it this way. It's like a key is handed to you after logging in.

Then you can use this key to do all sorts of actions in the application instead of constantly being asked for credentials. The key is the proof needed by the app to know it is still you. Think of it as opening locked doors when doing an action.

Now that you have the basics of JWT, let's get more technical.

What Does It Actually Look Like?

Well, it's a string. Literally just a string. It is divided into three parts: the header, the payload, and the signature. See the example below:

'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJub29ibWFzdGVyNjkiLCJyb2xlIjoidXNlciIsIm1lc3NhZ2UiOiJUaG9yJ3Mgc2VjcmV0IGVuZW15IiwicGFzc3dvcmQiOiJJIGxvdmUgeW91IDMwMDAiLCJleHAiOjE3OTU1OTkxODB9.kPlUDMKpcAw9izsnV3VBkF3kyInMwe4oPmdoqSas2vU'

If you look closely, the three parts are separated by two dots. In this example, we are using HS256 as the signing algorithm:

  • Header: Contains information about the token, such as the signing algorithm used.
  • Payload: The data the token carries such as the user's ID.
  • Signature: The part that helps verify whether the token has been tampered with.

You may ask, how could someone tamper with it? It looks like it's already encrypted. This is also what I thought but it turns out it's not.

The payload is encoded, not encrypted.

Encoding simply transforms data into a different format so it's easier to transport, while encrypting transforms data so that only someone with the key can decrypt and read it. Anyone who gets their hands on a JWT can decode it back into a readable format.

So if JWT is encoded, couldn't an attacker modify its payload? How can the backend trust it now?

Remember the third part of JWT? The signature helps the backend verify whether the token has been tampered with. The backend recreates the signature using the same signing algorithm and signing key. If the recreated signature doesn't match, the token is rejected.

But what if the attacker changes the signature too?

They can't without the signing key. They may know which algorithm is being used, but they don't have the environment key needed to create a valid signature (yet another reason why we don't commit our .env secrets to Git!)

So, How Does the Backend Use JWT?

It starts when a user logs in. After a successful login, the backend issues a JWT. Whenever the user does something in the app, the JWT is attached to the request. The backend verifies the signature and relevant claims (i.e. expiration date). If everything checks out, the request proceeds to the next step.

In this example, JWT solves authentication across multiple requests without having to ask the user to log in every single time an action is made.

But remember, this only solves authentication. It doesn't mean the user is allowed to do everything. There should be limitations and that's where the last section comes in.

A Few Things To Note

Authentication is not the same as authorization. JWT helps establish a user's identity, which is part of authentication. Authorization, on the other hand, determines whether that user has permission to perform a particular action or access a resource.

Next, tokens shouldn't last forever. In fact, a short-lived JWT is preferred. Expiration time is a must so that stolen tokens don't remain valid indefinitely. That's where refresh tokens come in (you can look them up if you want to learn more).

Lastly, don't put sensitive information like passwords in the JWT payload. Remember, it is only encoded, not encrypted. Utilize security techniques such as using HTTPS only and proper token storage.

That's pretty much it. I was actually planning on adding more but I feel like that would be too technical. Hopefully, this article shed more light about how JWT works. Breaking it down certainly helped me and I hope it did the same to you.

Just remember, whenever you log in, just know that web apps are always checking your identity on every single action you do. They are checking. Always checking.

PS. I drew some of the illustrations here by recreating drawings I found online and others from libraries I downloaded. I think this is the closest I could get to making a blog post feel like a YouTube explainer video, so I hope that goal was achieved.

By the way, try decoding the JWT string example above. If you do, then congrats on discovering a Marvel easter egg! That'll be your reward for making it this far. Have a good one!

Hoi hoi!

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript, OSS, and getting lost in forests of generated code. 🌳

Six months ago, I compared four OpenAPI code generators in this article 👇

Which OpenAPI Codegen Should You Choose? openapi-typescript vs hey-api vs Orval vs Kubb
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
May 20

Which OpenAPI Codegen Should You Choose? openapi-typescript vs hey-api vs Orval vs Kubb

#typescript #openapi #frontend #webdev
62 reactions Comments 15 comments
18 min read

I chose Hey API.

I'm still using it in production, and I'm pretty happy with it.

But Kubb has changed a lot with v5! 🚀

Faster generation? Better clients? A new plugin architecture?

Oh no. Time to go back into the forest. 🌳🌳🌳

Let's see what has changed!

🎯 TL;DR

Library Why I would choose it
openapi-typescript Types with minimal generated code
Hey API Clean SDKs and comfortable DX
Orval Flexible client, query, and mock generation
Kubb v5 Extensible code generation with much-improved clients

I'm keeping Hey API in my existing projects.

But for my next project? Kubb looks quite tempting. 👀

🕰️ Six months later

Here are the versions I tested (Kubb plugins have their own versions) 👇

Library May 2026 November 2026
openapi-typescript 7.13.0 7.13.0
Hey API 0.96.1 0.99.0
Orval 8.8.1 8.48.0
Kubb 4.37.2 5.20.2

Kubb had a major architectural overhaul, while Hey API and Orval continued improving their existing ecosystems.

Let's see what that actually means for us.

🏎️ How fast are they now?

For this investigation, I generated a synthetic OpenAPI specification using drf-spectacular.

  • 1,200 operations
  • 484 component schemas
  • 51,878 lines
  • Approximately 1.28 MB

I reran the previous versions using this new specification.

All measurements below are from the same Ryzen 9 7900 machine running WSL2 and Node.js 26. Each result is the median of eight measured executions after one warm-up.

Types only

Generating 484 shared component schemas

Library Time Peak RSS (max)
openapi-typescript 438 ms 191 MiB
Hey API 527 ms 240 MiB
Orval 866 ms 145 MiB
Kubb 337 ms 156 MiB

Wait, Kubb?! 😳

Types + Fetch SDK

I benchmarked both old and current versions on the same synthetic schema and machine.

Library Old version Current version Reduction
Hey API 7,406 ms 1,329 ms 82.1%
Orval 3,457 ms 1,723 ms 50.2%
Kubb 6,236 ms 1,155 ms 81.5%

That's a massive improvement for both Hey API and Kubb.

openapi-typescript took 751 ms to generate the full operation types, but it uses a generic runtime client rather than generating an SDK for every endpoint, so I've kept it separate.

Generation scopes and output structures still differ, and these aren't measurements against the original production API.

Also, generation isn't everything. A single TypeScript compilation took approximately 2.44 seconds for Hey API and 3.80 seconds for Kubb.

Fast generation doesn't necessarily mean faster everything.

Still, impressive work! 🚀

🌳 How big is the forest?

Here's the generated output for the full specification.

Library Files Source size
openapi-typescript 1 1.45 MB
Hey API 16 1.78 MB
Orval 1,926 2.18 MB
Kubb 2,897 3.13 MB

A house, a small town, a forest, and a very ambitious forest.

openapi-typescript/
  types.ts

hey-api/
  types.gen.ts
  sdk.gen.ts
  client.gen.ts
  client/
  core/

orval/
  api.ts
  schemas/

kubb/
  clients/
  types/
  .kubb/

I still prefer Hey API's relatively compact structure.

But Kubb's distributed files aren't necessarily a bad thing. Smaller individual files can make generated code easier to navigate and review.

These are generated source sizes, by the way—not application bundle sizes.

🧑‍💻 Let's actually call an API

Suppose we have three endpoints 👇

GET  /users
GET  /users/{id}
POST /users

openapi-typescript

Using its official companion, openapi-fetch

const client = createClient<paths>({
  baseUrl: BASE_URL,
});

client.GET("/users", {
  params: { query: { limit: 2 } },
});

client.GET("/users/{id}", {
  params: { path: { id: "1" } },
});

client.POST("/users", {
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

No generated function for every endpoint.

Just typed URLs, HTTP methods, and a generic client.

Small. Simple. Useful. 👍

Hey API 

getUsers({
  query: { limit: 2 },
});

getUser({
  path: { id: "1" },
});

createUser({
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

This is one of the main reasons I chose Hey API.

I don't need to remember the argument order of 1,200 functions.

Just query, path, and body.

My little brain is happy. 😸🧠

Orval

With useNamedParameters: true

getUsers({ limit: 2 });

getUser({ id: "1" });

createUser({
  id: "1",
  name: "Ada",
});

Request options can be passed separately, and custom mutators allow you to centralize transport logic. 👍

Kubb v5 

getUsers({
  query: { limit: 2 },
});

getUser({
  path: { id: "1" },
});

createUser({
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

This looks familiar. 👀

Kubb now gives me the consistent request structure I like in Hey API.

One of my previous concerns is gone. 😸🚀

⚠️ What happens when things explode?

Let's say our API returns

  • 200: User[]
  • 400: { message: string }
  • 409: { conflict: string }

I like result-based error handling, but sometimes I also want exceptions.

More importantly, I want TypeScript to know which error I'm dealing with.

openapi-fetch 

const result = await list();

if (
  result.response.status === 400 &&
  result.error !== undefined &&
  "message" in result.error
) {
  console.log(result.error.message);
}

Hey API 

const result = await list();

if (
  result.response?.status === 400 &&
  result.error !== undefined &&
  "message" in result.error
) {
  console.log(result.error.message);
}

You get typed error responses, but checking the nested HTTP status alone doesn't narrow the error body.

Orval 

const result = await list();

if (result.status === 400) {
  console.log(result.data.message);
}

if (result.status === 409) {
  console.log(result.data.conflict);
}

Nice!

The top-level status acts as a discriminant. 😸

Kubb v5 

const result = await getUsers({
  throwOnError: false,
});

if (result.status === 400) {
  if ("message" in result.error) {
    console.log(result.error.message);
  }
}

Kubb also provides status-based narrowing. The additional guard handles the possible empty error body. 👍

To throw or not to throw

  • Hey API 
await getUsers({
  throwOnError: true,
});
  • Kubb 
await getUsers({
  throwOnError: true,
});

Hey API defaults to result-style HTTP errors in the tested SDK; Kubb defaults to throwing. Both let me choose.

Or, with Kubb

const users = await getUsers({
  throwOnError: false,
}).unwrap();

I particularly like this little .unwrap().

Give me the data or reject. Thank you very much!

There are still differences in what each client considers an error.

Behavior Hey API Kubb
Result-style HTTP errors ✅ ✅
Configurable throwing ✅ ✅
Status-discriminated result — ✅
.unwrap() — ✅
Network failure in nonthrowing mode Returned error in tests Rejected in tests

Nonthrowing HTTP mode doesn't mean nothing can throw!

🪝 What about TanStack Query?

All four have a way to integrate with TanStack Query.

// openapi-react-query
$api.queryOptions("get", "/users");

// Hey API
getUsersOptions();

// Orval
getGetUsersQueryOptions();

// Kubb
getUsersQueryOptions();

One interesting difference appeared in the runtime tests:

Library HTTP 400 in tested query configuration
openapi-react-query Rejects
Hey API Rejects
Orval Resolves by default
Kubb Rejects by default

TanStack Query needs a rejected promise to recognize a failed request.

For Orval's tested Fetch configuration, enabling override.fetch.forceSuccessResponse: true changes that behavior.

Not a deal-breaker. Just something worth configuring before your query happily reports that everything is fine while your API is on fire. 🔥

🤯 The enum problem, again

Remember those little enums that caused so much trouble last time?

They're back.

Consider these schema fragments:

BlankEnum:
  type: string
  enum: [""]

NullEnum:
  enum: [null]

Here's what happened:

Case openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb
Empty-string enum (3.0 fixture) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Null-only enum (3.1 fixture) ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅

Kubb's previous blank-enum issue is fixed! 🎉

Its v4 already handled the tested null-only case correctly, so that isn't a new v5 improvement.

Interestingly, Hey API still has a problem with the null-only enum.

type NullEnum = never;

Oops.

Adding type: 'null' fixes the TypeScript type, but the generated Zod validator can still accept unrelated values.

The verified workaround for this OpenAPI 3.1 case is:

NullEnum:
  type: "null"

Now we get the correct type and validator:

type NullEnum = null;

const zNullEnum = z.null();

There's also an existing upstream issue.

It's a specific edge case, not a general problem with nullable properties.
But this is why I test generated types instead of simply trusting them.

🛡️ Type safety at runtime

TypeScript is wonderful. Unfortunately, my backend doesn't care. 😹

All four default clients accepted invalid response data in my tests. With runtime validation, all four rejected it.

Library Validation
openapi-typescript Manual
Hey API Generated Zod
Orval Generated Zod
Kubb Generated Zod

Encoding and decoding

Kubb has another interesting feature: directional transformations.

const result = await postTimestamp({
  body: { at: new Date() },
});

const date: Date = result.data.at;

With inferred: 'codec' and a custom datetime printer, Kubb generated the ISO string ↔ Date transformations and integrated them into the client.

These are directional Zod transforms, not native bidirectional z.codec objects.

Less glue code. Happy cats. 🐈

Server-Sent Events

Both Hey API and Kubb handled typed SSE in my tests.

// Hey API
const { stream } = await heyEvents();

for await (const event of stream) {
  console.log(event.value);
}

// Kubb
const { stream } = await kubbEvents();

for await (const event of stream) {
  console.log(event.data.value);
}

Different wrappers, same typed streaming goodness.

🧰 The ecosystem

Feature openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb
Fetch ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Axios — ✅ ✅ ✅
React Query ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
SWR — ✅ ✅ ✅
Zod generation — ✅ ✅ ✅
Faker / MSW — ✅ ✅ ✅
Native custom plugins — ✅ — ✅

These are official integrations and companions, not necessarily built-in features. Other extension mechanisms exist.

One correction from my previous comparison: Hey API also supports Faker, MSW, and SWR. I verified Faker/MSW behavior and SWR generation.

The ecosystems are getting crowded. In a good way! 😸

🏗️ Kubb v5: More than an OpenAPI generator?

This is where Kubb gets interesting.

OpenAPI
   ↓
Unified AST
   ↓
Plugins + Resolvers + Macros
   ↓
Generated code

Kubb v5 lets plugins share a normalized AST instead of independently parsing the specification.

But what does that actually give us?

Resolvers

Let's say my project requires an Api prefix and .model.ts filenames.

import { pluginTs, resolverTs } from '@kubb/plugin-ts';

pluginTs({
  resolver: {
    name(name) {
      return `Api${resolverTs.name(name)}`;
    },
    file: {
      baseName({ name, extname }) {
        return `${name}.model${extname}`;
      },
    },
  },
});

The result?

- GetUsersOptions
+ ApiGetUsersOptions

Even better, the Fetch plugin automatically imports the renamed type from the renamed file.

No regex magic. No broken imports. Strict TypeScript compilation passed.

Macros

I also tested removing descriptions from TypeScript output while preserving them in Zod output.

It worked. Each plugin can transform its own AST without affecting the others.

Kubb Kit and Registry

Kubb Kit lets developers build custom generators using the same infrastructure as official plugins.

And the Kubb Registry lets the community distribute extensions.

Kubb registry · Kubb

The list of Kubb extensions that the Kubb CLI, Kubb Studio and kubb.dev read. It is a set of static JSON documents under one base URL.

kubb.dev

Hey API also supports custom plugins, so extensibility isn't unique to Kubb.

But the combination of shared AST, resolvers, macros, and Kit makes Kubb particularly interesting for building a company-wide generation platform.

🤖 AI can grow a forest overnight

AI makes generating code faster. Keeping it consistent? Not so much.

Imagine five AI agents building five features, each inventing different API wrappers and error handling.

Congratulations! Five different forests. 🌳🌴🌲🎋🌵

Why keep telling AI the same rules when we can encode them into a shared generator?

Let AI help build the plugins. Let deterministic codegen enforce the conventions.

One shared plugin can serve ten projects instead of ten AI agents reinventing the same thing.

Maybe the best use of AI isn't generating more code. It's building better tools that generate code for us.

And that's exactly why Kubb's architecture caught my attention.

🌱 Maintaining the forest

I also tested how generated code changes when the API evolves.

Library Changed files Added / removed lines
openapi-typescript 1 +2 / −2
Hey API 3 +9 / −9
Orval 3 +14 / −14
Kubb 6 +59 / −59

These results are from renaming one operationId.

All four generated identical output with unchanged input, and breaking schema changes were caught by application type checks.

More files aren't necessarily worse. Just keep your forest under control! 🌳

🤝 Kubb Studio

Kubb also introduced Kubb Studio, a separate collaboration service.

Kubb Studio · Generate typed clients from your API spec

Generate TypeScript clients, TanStack Query hooks and Zod schemas from your API spec on your own machines. Review every change, then ship from CI. Start free.

kubb.studio

It offers UI-based plugin configuration, generated-file comments, and npm snapshots through GitHub Actions.

That could help frontend teams work against upcoming backend contracts before release.

I haven't tested it hands-on yet, but it's an interesting direction!

📓 Side by side

openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb v5
Approach Types SDK Configurable generators Extensible generators
Request style Typed URL Named options Configurable Named options
Output Minimal Compact Configurable Distributed
Errors Result Result / Throw Status / Throw Result / Throw / Unwrap
Validation Manual Generated Generated Generated
Extensions Scripts / AST Plugins Transformers / hooks Kit / Resolvers / Macros

🚀 Back out of the forest

Six months ago, I chose Hey API. And I'm keeping it.

But Kubb v5 surprised me.

It's faster, its clients have improved, and its architecture offers something beyond a ready-made SDK.

In the AI era, I think shared development foundations matter more than ever.

For my next large frontend project, I'd love to give Kubb a try.

Six months ago, I wanted a smaller forest.

Now, I want to design how it grows.

Before AI plants another million trees. 🌳🤖

Thanks for reading! 🙌💚

Inside APIC

The complete engineering story behind the free, private, on-device photo studio from Akhouri Systems

Eleven tools. Zero uploads. Every pixel stays on your device.

Live product: apic-studio.vercel.app

Keynote opener

For years the deal with online image tools has been the same: upload your photo, wait for a server, pay per image, hope for the best.

We built APIC to retire that deal.

APIC (Advanced Image Processing Center) is a free online photo editor, background remover, object remover, AI upscaler, image converter and compressor. It runs entirely in your browser. AI models download once, get cached on your device, and from then on your photos are processed locally.

This post is the full tour, inch by inch. How each tool works, which models and algorithms power it, and why we made the engineering decisions we did.

If you came here looking for a free remove.bg alternative, a background remover with no upload, or a private online photo editor, you are in the right place.

The architecture in one picture 

 Your photo (never leaves the device)
        |
        v
 +-----------------------------------------------------------+
 |  Browser tab: APIC Studio                                 |
 |                                                           |
 |  Canvas pixel pipeline --> Edit / Advanced / Resize       |
 |  Format engine ----------> PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, ICO, PDF |
 |  Web Workers ------------> ONNX Runtime Web               |
 |                              |-- WebAssembly (everywhere) |
 |                              |-- WebGPU (when available)  |
 |  Model cache ------------> downloaded once, reused        |
 |  Recent work ------------> saved on this device           |
 +-----------------------------------------------------------+
        |
        v
 Export: transparent PNG, WebP, JPEG, PDF, ZIP

Heavy AI work runs inside Web Workers, so the interface stays responsive while a model is thinking. ONNX Runtime Web runs the models on WebAssembly by default and upgrades to WebGPU on devices that support it.

Tool 1 to 3: Edit, Advanced, Resize

Edit

The everyday toolkit: brightness, contrast, saturation, blur, rotate, flip, crop with ratio presets, and straighten.

It also has Hide area: select a rectangle or an ellipse (the ellipse is better for faces) and blur or pixelate it. Use it to cover faces, licence plates, card numbers and anything else private before you share an image.

Advanced: the pro colour suite

This is where we stopped treating colour as a slider and started treating it as a pipeline. Every adjustment runs through one ordered pixel pipeline:

exposure (linear light)
  -> black / white point
  -> gamma
  -> RGB curve -> per-channel curves
  -> white balance (temperature / tint)
  -> shadows / highlights
  -> vibrance
  -> HSL mixer (8 bands)
  -> 3-way colour grading
  -> fade
  -> clarity
  -> sharpen
  -> vignette
  -> grain

What you get on top of it:

  • A live histogram
  • RGB curves with per-channel control
  • An 8-band HSL mixer (Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Aqua, Blue, Purple, Magenta)
  • 3-way colour grading
  • 3D LUT export: a 33 x 33 x 33 .cube LUT of your whole grade, ready for video tools such as DaVinci Resolve and Premiere

That last one matters. You can grade a still in the browser and carry the same look into video.

Resize

Exact pixel or percentage resizing. When shrinking, the resampling is built to keep fine detail crisp instead of blurring or producing moiré, with a final high-quality pass onto the exact target size.

Tool 4: Remove BG, the on-device cut-out engine

This is the feature people search for, so we over-engineered it.

The pipeline

  1. General-purpose segmentation with IS-Net (DIS) at 1024 x 1024. It handles people, products, animals, objects and logos, not only portraits.
  2. Mask cleanup. Noise specks and pinholes are removed.
  3. Edge snapping with a guided filter. The mask is snapped onto the real edges of the photo, limited to a narrow band around the model's edge. It can sharpen the boundary but never invent or delete real regions.
  4. Blur-Fusion foreground estimation. This removes background colour bleeding into edge pixels, so you get no coloured halo on a new backdrop.
  5. Original resolution preserved. The output keeps your original pixels in the interior. It is not a downscaled approximation.

If the main AI model can't load (offline or blocked), APIC falls back to a MediaPipe person segmenter, still at full resolution, so you always get a result.

Four quality tiers

Tier Model Download Best for
Lite U²-Netp (320 px) ~5 MB Instant results, low-power devices
Fast IS-Net, quantized (1024 px) ~44 MB Everyday speed and quality
Great IS-Net, full (1024 px) ~176 MB High accuracy
Best (optional) BiRefNet, WebGPU build ~520 MB (fp16) to 1 GB Maximum quality on capable hardware

Models download once and are cached. If a download fails, APIC retries automatically and offers a Retry button. If you are offline, it tells you plainly: connect once so the model can download.

Touch-up and replacement

  • Restore / Erase brush with adjustable size to fix edges by hand
  • One-click backgrounds: white, black, a blurred copy of your photo, or any custom colour
  • Export as a transparent PNG or WebP

Tool 5: Remove Object, on-device inpainting

Paint over a person, sign or blemish. An on-device inpainting model fills the area to match its surroundings.

  • Standard engine: MI-GAN, fast and light
  • Ultra engine: LaMa, for larger or more complex areas on desktop-class devices

Some details we care about:

  • The network runs at a manageable resolution, then the fill is upscaled and composited back, so everything outside the hole stays untouched.
  • Because an upscaled fill is softer than the original photo, a gentle unsharp mask is applied to match texture.

Tool 6: Convert

Convert between PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, ICO and PDF.

  • HEIC and HEIF input from iPhones, decoded on your device
  • Multi-image to one multi-page PDF
  • Use PNG or WebP to keep transparency after background removal

Tool 7: Compress, hit the file size you need

Most compressors make you guess a quality number. APIC asks for the target size instead.

Under the hood it runs a binary search over encoder quality (roughly from 5% to 98%), keeping the highest quality whose output still fits under your limit. Need a photo under 200 KB for an upload form? Type 200 and you are done.

Tool 8: AI Tools

All on-device. Every result can be undone with Ctrl+Z.

  • Auto-enhance (one click): levels, exposure and a touch of colour
  • Smart crop: detect the subject and crop to it, free-form or to 1:1, 4:5, 3:4, 4:3, 16:9 and more. If no subject is found, it falls back to a centre crop and tells you.
  • AI upscale, 2x or 4x:
    • Max accuracy: Real-ESRGAN x4plus (~64 MB)
    • Fast: general-x4v3 (~5 MB)
    • Phones and tablets default to Fast so mobile stays smooth.

Tool 9 to 11: Layers, Social, Visual Intelligence

Layers

Compose multiple elements into one image.

Social

Exact-size presets for profile pictures, banners, covers, posts and stories across Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, X, TikTok, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Snapchat, Threads, Bluesky, Discord, Twitch, Spotify and more.

  • Drag and zoom to frame your photo
  • Safe-zone guides show where each platform crops or overlays your image
  • Download one size, or a ZIP of every size for a network
  • File sizes are kept under each platform's limit automatically

Visual Intelligence

Preflight checks that flag size, quality and privacy issues before you share.

Batch Studio

Process many images at once and get one ZIP:

  • Remove backgrounds in bulk
  • Resize by longest side or percentage
  • Convert formats
  • Set quality or a target KB

All of it runs on your device.

Privacy is the product

Typical online tool APIC
Uploads your photo to a server Processes it on your device
Per-image credits and paywalls Free, no per-image credits
Account required to start Works without an account (Google sign-in is optional)
Needs a connection every time Models are cached after first download
Online only Windows app (APIC for PC) for fully offline use

There is also a "Recent work" shelf that is saved on your device and can be cleared at any time.

The polish layer

  • Dark and light themes that apply before first paint, so there is no flash
  • A responsive layout tuned for phones, tablets and desktops, with mobile-aware model defaults
  • Honest, readable error messages instead of stack traces
  • Undo on AI actions

Why we build like this

At Akhouri Systems, we think powerful software should be:

  1. Private by design, not by policy
  2. Free where it can be, with no credit-meter anxiety
  3. Fast on the hardware you already own
  4. Explained in the open, which is why this post exists

The browser is a serious computer now. It runs neural networks, GPU compute and real colour science. We just decided to use all of it for you.

Try APIC in 10 seconds

  1. Open apic-studio.vercel.app
  2. Drop in a photo
  3. Choose Remove BG and press Remove
  4. Export a clean transparent PNG

Then explore the rest of the eleven tools.

Build something. Ship it. Keep going.

Every product on this list started as a blank file and a bad first draft. Our background remover used to be a tiny selfie-only model that gave blurry output. We rebuilt it around a 1024-pixel general-purpose model, edge-aware refinement and full-resolution output.

That is the whole secret: ship, listen, rebuild, repeat.

Whatever you are building, keep building. 🚀

FAQ

Is APIC really free?
Yes. There are no paid tiers and no per-image credits.

Are my photos uploaded to a server?
No. Editing, converting, compressing, resizing, background removal and object removal run on your device.

How does the AI background remover work?
It runs a segmentation model in your browser using WebAssembly, with WebGPU for the optional heavy model. Models download once and are cached.

Why is the first AI run slower?
The model has to download the first time. After that it is cached and runs start much faster.

Can I compress an image to a specific file size?
Yes. Set a target size and APIC searches for the best quality that fits.

Does it open iPhone HEIC photos?
Yes, and it converts them on your device.

Is there an offline version?
Yes. APIC for PC is a Windows app that runs offline.

Follow Akhouri Systems

Follow us on dev.to for more engineering deep dives, and tell us in the comments: which APIC internals should we break down next? The BiRefNet WebGPU path? The 3D LUT export? The guided-filter edge snapping?

Open APIC

A browser benchmark can produce an impressive number while measuring only the easiest part of the experience. Timing one inference call can hide runtime loading, model transfer, compilation, initialization, output readback, and the work the surrounding interface must still perform.

For a feature used once during a form submission, those costs may matter more than its tenth inference. For a continuously running camera feature, repeated inference may dominate. The benchmark needs to match the interaction.

This walkthrough builds a small LiteRT.js harness that can request Wasm or WebGPU execution for the same model. It records the phases separately, preserves raw samples, and keeps backend configuration distinct from user-perceived speed. It does not assume that requesting the GPU means every operation ran there, or that a result from one machine predicts every device.

Fix the workload before changing the accelerator

The companion pins @litertjs/core to 2.6.0 and downloads Google’s MobileNetV2 demo model. The downloaded file is 14,020,256 bytes. Its SHA-256 is recorded in the supplied model manifest, so someone repeating the experiment can verify that the weights have not changed.

The harness uses one deterministic floating-point tensor. That makes the input identical across accelerator runs and avoids including image decoding in an inference-only measurement. It is deliberately not an image-recognition accuracy benchmark.

For a product evaluation, add a separate dataset of licensed images and a verified preprocessing pipeline. A model can return finite numbers for incorrectly normalized input. Output shape and absence of exceptions are useful smoke checks, not evidence that the classifier understands the images.

Keep initialization visible

LiteRT.js separates loading its runtime from loading and compiling a model. Fetch the model explicitly when you want its transfer time to remain visible.

await loadLiteRt("/wasm/");
const response = await fetch("/model.tflite");
if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Model download failed.");
const bytes = new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());
const model = await loadAndCompile(bytes, { accelerator });

The complete harness timestamps each phase and hashes the downloaded bytes outside the compilation interval. It reads the model’s input details rather than silently assuming a tensor layout. The example rejects models that do not have a single float32 input.

The supplied preparation command copies the runtime assets from the installed package. This keeps the JavaScript and Wasm versions aligned. Loading JavaScript from one release and Wasm from an unversioned CDN URL would introduce an avoidable variable.

Figure 1. Change the execution request while keeping the model and input fixed.

Include output readback in the timed operation

The example measures a result that JavaScript can actually inspect:

const start = performance.now();
const outputs = await model.run(input);
try {
  const data = await outputs[0].data();
  for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
    if (!Number.isFinite(Number(data[i]))) {
      throw new Error("Non-finite output.");
    }
  }
  return performance.now() - start;
} finally {
  outputs.forEach(output => output.delete());
}

Output transfer can matter when comparing an accelerator with CPU execution. If you exclude it, label the metric accordingly and explain why the application can avoid that transfer.

Release input tensors and the compiled model after the benchmark as well. Otherwise, repeated experiments can accumulate resources and change the environment you think you are holding constant.

Separate the first run from the warm runs

The harness records the first inference, performs three additional warmups, then retains ten measured samples. It reports the median without discarding the underlying observations.

Recorded value Question it helps answer
Runtime load time How long did runtime initialization take?
Model fetch time and bytes What did obtaining the weights cost?
Compilation time What did preparing this backend cost?
First inference What happens before the runtime is warm?
Ten warm samples How variable is repeated execution here?
Output sample and length Did both runs produce comparable numerical output?

Ten samples are enough to inspect the harness, not to make a strong population-level tail-latency claim. Repeat whole sessions, alternate backend order, and report device conditions before drawing a performance conclusion.

Reload the page between accelerators. A reload resets the page’s runtime but does not necessarily clear the HTTP cache, operating-system caches, or driver caches. Describe the cache condition rather than calling every reload a cold start.

Check what WebGPU actually means in the run

The WebGPU branch first requests an adapter. If none is returned, it records an unsupported result instead of inventing a zero-duration measurement or quietly labeling a Wasm run as GPU execution.

LiteRT’s documentation notes that unsupported accelerated operations can fall back to CPU. Therefore, the requested accelerator is configuration evidence, not a complete execution profile. Capture available adapter information and use runtime diagnostics when making claims about where computation occurred.

A software adapter in a headless environment is also a different subject from a physical laptop GPU. Keep that distinction in the results table.

Run and interpret the experiment

From the companion’s lab directory, run npm ci, npm run prepare:model, and npm run build. Start npm run preview, open /benchmark.html, and run one accelerator per reload. Preserve the JSON output from each run with the browser and machine details.

The Wasm harness completed in Headless Chrome 153 on a virtualized Linux host: it accepted a [1, 3, 224, 224] input and returned 1,000 finite values through the first run, warmups, and ten measured runs. The raw JSON is included as an execution check. GPU execution was disabled in that environment, so these observations establish no WebGPU-versus-Wasm speed ranking. Hardware runs and an application-level responsiveness measurement remain necessary before recommending a backend for a real feature.

For the latter, measure an actual interaction while inference runs: typing into a field, opening a panel, or scrolling through results. A fast model invocation can coexist with a poor page experience if preprocessing or rendering blocks the main thread.

Which cost dominates your feature: obtaining the first useful answer, repeatedly processing frames, or keeping the surrounding interface responsive?

References

  • LiteRT.js overview and execution
  • LiteRT.js getting started
  • Client-side AI performance
  • Model caching guidance

articles.title: Stop Tweeting Into the Void: The Software Engineer's Guide to Turning X Into an Inbound Career Engine
articles.description: A tactical, 10-minute masterclass for developers on using X (Twitter) effectively. Learn how to escape the zero-follower ghost town, build public proof of work, connect with core maintainers and founders, and generate inbound career opportunities without becoming a cringey influencer.
articles.body_html:
Almost every software engineer who joins X (Twitter) follows the exact same tragic script:

You hear that tech Twitter is where open-source authors hang out, where startup founders recruit, and where indie hackers build six-figure businesses in public.

Inspired, you create an account. You spend twenty minutes picking a clean handle. You upload a nice profile picture, and then you compose your very first tweet:

"Excited to start learning Rust and distributed systems today! Day 1 starts now. 🦀🚀 #100DaysOfCode #Rust"

You hit send. You wait.

An hour passes: zero likes, zero retweets, twelve impressions.

Two days later, you share a link to a blog post you spent sixteen hours writing: zero likes, one bot retweet, twenty impressions.

By day five, posting feels like shouting into an empty concrete warehouse. You feel awkward, self-conscious, and slightly embarrassed. You conclude that X is a rigged game reserved strictly for loud influencers, crypto shills, and people with blue checkmarks who tweet generic motivational quotes every morning at 7:00 AM.

So you close the tab and return to sending your resume into the cold, automated applicant tracking system (ATS) black hole on LinkedIn.

Here is the truth that nobody tells junior and mid-level developers:

You were not failing because the platform is broken. You were failing because you used a discovery platform like a megaphone instead of an operating system.

When used correctly, X is not social media. It is the most powerful public permissionless API for your engineering career.

Founders don't hire engineers off job boards when they can find someone who has spent six months documenting their architectural decisions in public. Open-source maintainers don't review PRs from strangers as quickly as they review PRs from people who have been asking intelligent questions in their replies for weeks.

Here is the engineering playbook for turning X into an inbound career engine without sacrificing your dignity or becoming an engagement farmer.

1. The Fatal Developer Mistake: Broadcasting vs Engaging

To understand why your early tweets get zero traction, you must understand how the recommendation algorithm treats accounts with zero social graph history.

When you create a new account, the algorithm has zero data on who you are, what domain you specialize in, or whether your content provides signal or spam.

If you tweet into the empty feed:

[Your New Account] ──► Broadcasts Tweet ──► Delivered to: 0 Followers (The Void)

Nobody sees it because nobody follows you, and the algorithm has no statistical reason to push an unproven account into the algorithmic "For You" timeline.

Broadcasting only works after you have accumulated an audience. In the beginning, broadcasting is a guaranteed failure.

The Inverted Strategy: The High-Signal Reply Engine

How do you get your first 500 high-quality followers, peers, and industry connections?

You do not write original tweets. You write high-signal replies on other people's tweets.

Think of it as piggybacking on established network bandwidth:

  1. When a prominent framework creator, staff engineer, or founder with 50,000 followers posts an architectural problem or an update, their tweet receives 30,000 views within two hours.
  2. 95% of the replies are low-effort noise: "Great point!", "Totally agree", or a generic reaction GIF.
  3. If you post a thoughtful, technically substantive reply (a benchmark you ran, an edge-case insight, a clean code snippet, or an informed counter-argument), your reply floats straight to the top of the comment tree.
  4. Hundreds of engineers reading that thread see your technical competence. They click your profile.

Your replies are your free billboard in high-traffic engineering neighborhoods.

2. Profile Architecture: Building a High-Converting Landing Page

When an engineer or engineering manager clicks your profile from an insightful reply, you have approximately four seconds before they hit the back button.

Most developers treat their profile like a casual social bio:
"Coffee lover ☕ | Full stack dev | Living life | Views are my own"

This bio tells a visitor absolutely nothing about your technical leverage, your niche, or why they should follow you.

Treat your profile like a high-converting software landing page:

[Header Banner]   ──► Visual context of what you build (Terminal, Architecture, Product UI)
[Profile Avatar]  ──► Clear, friendly, high-contrast headshot
[Handle & Name]   ──► Real name + recognizable identity
[Bio]             ──► Niche + Proof of Work + Current Focus
[Pinned Tweet]    ──► Your absolute best project, case study, or technical thread
[Link]            ──► Personal site, GitHub, or live project (NEVER a generic Linktree)

The Anatomy of a High-Conversion Developer Bio

A great developer bio answers three questions in under 160 characters:

  1. What is your technical specialty? (e.g., Go backend, iOS Compose, Distributed Systems)
  2. What have you built or where do you work? (Proof of work)
  3. What are you building or exploring right now? (Current journey)

Weak Bio:

"Software engineer passionate about tech. Love React and JavaScript. Let's connect!"

High-Converting Bio:

"Building distributed storage in Go. Ex-Shopify intern. Writing about database internals and high-throughput systems. Working on @myopenSourceDb."

Notice the difference: The second bio establishes domain authority, clear interests, and proof of work in two seconds.

The Pinned Tweet: Your Living Technical Portfolio

Nobody browses your personal portfolio site unless they already have a reason to care.

Your Pinned Tweet is where you force that interest.

Your pinned tweet should never be a random joke or an announcement from three years ago. It should be a mini-case study of your best work:

  • A 45-second video recording of a performant UI or developer tool you built.
  • A deep technical breakdown of a hard concurrency bug you diagnosed.
  • An open-source library you released, complete with benchmarks and the GitHub repository link.

When recruiters, hiring managers, and prospective collaborators land on your profile, your pinned tweet instantly proves that you write production code and understand software systems.

3. The 3-Tier "Proof of Work" Content Matrix

The biggest anxiety developers express about X is: "What do I actually tweet about? I'm not an expert, and I don't want to sound like a self-important guru."

The secret is to stop trying to be a teacher. Be a documentarian.

You do not need ten years of distributed systems experience to share valuable technical content. You only need to be one hour ahead of the developer who hasn't solved the bug you just spent all afternoon fixing.

The best technical accounts organize their content across three distinct tiers:

Tier 1: Daily Debugging & Micro-Learnings (60% of Content)

This is the bedrock of your consistency. It requires zero artificial brainstorming because it comes directly from your daily terminal session.

Every time you spend two hours debugging a bizarre issue, encountering an unexpected framework behavior, or learning a neat shell trick, you have content:

  • "Spent two hours debugging a memory leak in Go today. Turns out unbuffered channels block forever if the receiver exits early. Here is the 3-line fix with context timeouts."
  • "TIL: In Docker multi-stage builds, copying package.json before the source code saves 4 minutes of rebuild time on cached layers."

This is high-signal, authentic, and immediately relatable to fellow developers. It proves you are in the trenches writing code every single day.

Tier 2: Deep Technical Breakdown Threads (30% of Content)

Once or twice a month, synthesize your deeper investigations into a structured multi-tweet thread or long-form post.

Topics that consistently perform well in engineering circles include:

  1. Post-Mortems: Why a production service crashed and how your team resolved it.
  2. Architecture Comparisons: Why you chose SQLite over PostgreSQL for a local embedded service, backed by query benchmarks.
  3. Visual Explanations: Breaking down how a complex protocol (like WebSockets, Raft consensus, or JWTs) operates step-by-step.

Rules for High-Impact Technical Threads:

  • No Fluff Hooks: Avoid "Most developers get this wrong... a thread 🧵👇". Start with the punchline: "We reduced our Docker image from 1.2GB to 45MB by switching to distroless. Here are the 4 changes we made."
  • Show Real Code and Metrics: Include actual code snippets, memory graphs, and flame charts. Real artifacts build instant credibility.
  • Keep Each Tweet Self-Contained: Every post in the thread should teach a distinct mini-concept rather than being a sentence cut in half.

Tier 3: Milestones and Open Source Releases (10% of Content)

This is where you celebrate tangible outputs:

  • Releasing v1.0 of your open-source CLI tool.
  • Reaching 1,000 GitHub stars on a project.
  • Shipping an end-to-end side project with live user metrics.

Because 90% of your feed is pure technical substance, your community will enthusiastically support and amplify your milestone announcements.

4. How to Network with Senior Engineers and Founders Without Being Weird

Cold outreach in tech usually feels awkward and transactional.

Every senior engineer and tech founder receives dozens of generic LinkedIn messages every week:
"Hi, I saw you work at Stripe. Can you refer me for a Software Engineer role? Here is my resume."

These messages are deleted within three seconds. They provide zero value and demand an immediate, unearned favor.

X allows you to build warm, organic relationships in public before you ever enter private messages.

The 4-Step Relationship Pipeline

Here is how smart developers turn strangers into mentors, collaborators, and employers:

Step 1: Intelligent Public Observation

Identify 10 to 15 engineers, maintainers, and engineering managers whose work you genuinely admire. Follow them and add them to a private X List titled "Core Network".

Step 2: Value-Add Interaction

When they post a technical dilemma or ask for feedback, do not reply with generic praise. Provide genuine utility:

  • Test their open-source library on your machine and report a reproducible bug with a minimal reproduction repo.
  • Answer a niche documentation question they asked.
  • Share a relevant benchmark or technical paper that addresses their problem.

Step 3: Contribute to Their Projects

If they maintain an open-source tool, submit a clean PR that improves documentation, fixes a failing test, or adds a requested feature. When they merge it, tweet a genuine shoutout thanking them for maintaining the repository.

Step 4: The Frictionless Direct Message

Now, when you reach out in their DMs, you are not a faceless stranger asking for a handout. You are a competent engineer who has provided consistent value:

"Hey Sarah, really loved your thread on database sharding last week. I noticed your team at Scale is building out the distributed cache layer. I built a small Raft-based cache in Go last month (linked in my pinned tweet). If you're looking for someone who loves low-level systems and distributed state, I'd love to chat whenever you have 5 minutes."

The response rate to this message is astronomical compared to cold job boards because your technical competence was proven before the conversation even began.

5. Daily Habits: The 20-Minute Developer Routine

You do not need to spend four hours a day glued to your timeline. In fact, doing so will destroy your coding focus and productivity.

The most effective technical creators on X use a strict, time-boxed 20-minute daily routine:

1. Morning Triage (5 Minutes)

  • Open your notifications.
  • Reply to every technical question and comment on your previous posts.
  • Retweet or quote-tweet one piece of exceptional engineering work with your own technical commentary.

2. High-Signal Engagement (10 Minutes)

  • Open your curated private List of 15 key engineering leaders.
  • Leave three insightful, substantive replies on active technical discussions.
  • Focus purely on adding value, sharing code snippets, or clarifying architecture tradeoffs.

3. Document One Learning (5 Minutes)

  • Write and schedule one tweet based on what you worked on, read, or debugged during yesterday's coding session.
  • Keep it concrete: a command you ran, an error message you fixed, or an architectural realization.

Once your 20 minutes are up, close the application and write code. Your presence will compound automatically while you focus on deep work.

6. Three Toxic Traps to Avoid at All Costs

As you grow your network on X, you will inevitably be tempted by tactics that generate short-term engagement but destroy long-term engineering respect.

Avoid these three traps like production bugs:

Trap 1: The Engagement Farm

"React is DEAD. Agree or disagree? 👇"
"Which language is better: Python or Java? Comment below!"

These superficial polls and engagement-bait questions might generate algorithmic impressions, but they brand you as an amateur. Senior engineers, tech leads, and hiring managers look at this content with disdain. Protect your technical reputation above all else.

Trap 2: Endless Retweeting Without Commentary

If your profile consists of 80% retweets of other people's announcements, visitors have zero incentive to follow you. They will simply follow the original authors. Always add your own technical perspective or build your own original catalog of thoughts.

Trap 3: The Ghost Town Collapse

The first two months are the hardest. You will write posts that you spent two hours polishing, and they will receive five likes.

Do not stop.

The developers who win on X are not the ones who went viral on day three. They are the ones who published consistent proof of work for six months straight until their timeline became an undeniable public portfolio of engineering excellence.

The Mental Shift

Stop thinking of X as social media where you seek validation, followers, or likes.

X is an asynchronous public journal of your technical journey.

Every tweet documenting a bug fix is an indexed proof of your problem-solving ability.
Every deep thread breaking down an architecture choice is a public technical interview.
Every insightful reply to an open-source maintainer is a warm introduction into the top 1% of the engineering ecosystem.

When you treat your public presence as an engineering asset, you never have to scramble to polish a two-page PDF resume again. Opportunities, collaborations, and career breakthroughs will find you.

How has sharing your engineering journey online influenced your career or side projects? Have you connected with mentors, landed clients, or found open-source collaborators through tech Twitter, or does building in public still feel uncomfortable? Share your experiences and thoughts in the comments below.
