articles.body_html:
Your migration guide is on the web. An agent upgrading your library reads it only if it decides to search, and many runs never do. In my last round, whether an agent searched depended on the agent, on the model, and on something maintainers rarely think about: the language the user wrote the task in.

This is a follow-up to Coding agents keep installing the old version of your library. That piece was about where agents pick a version. This one asks what changes when the user doesn't write in English, and what a maintainer can do about it.

The test

Two upgrade tasks, each a small working project on the old version:

  • Hedera. "Update the Hedera SDK to the current supported version." The supported SDK moved from @hashgraph/sdk to @hiero-ledger/sdk, and the old name still shows as latest on npm, not deprecated. To pass, the agent has to find the new name.
  • Prisma. "Upgrade Prisma to version 8." Prisma 8 has no @prisma/client: the client is now @prisma/orm-postgres, while @prisma/client@latest still points to 7.

Four agents: Codex (GPT-6-Sol, effort low), Claude Code with Haiku 5.5, Kimi Code with K3.1, and Claude Code with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The same task text in English, Spanish, Ukrainian and Russian, with code and package names left in English. Three setups: no help, four lines in AGENTS.md, or a colleague's note about a similar case. Five runs per cell, a hidden grader for each run, 591 graded runs in total.

Searching decided the result

Without help, on Hedera, 13 of the 15 runs that searched the web found the new package. Of the 65 that didn't search, 7 did. npm view @hashgraph/sdk version says nothing about the move; the announcement does, and it's on the web.

The language changed whether the agent searched

Share of runs without help that actually upgraded the library:

Across both tasks: English 21 of 39, Spanish 19 of 39, Ukrainian 17 of 40, Russian 8 of 39. The gap between English and Russian is unlikely to be chance (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.005). Spanish and Ukrainian sit between the two.

Codex shows it most clearly. Runs without help in which it searched at least once, both tasks together:

With the task in English, Codex searched and passed Hedera 5 times out of 5. With the same task in Russian, it never searched and passed 0 of 5. I found the same pattern a few weeks earlier on different tasks, and I still don't know why it is Russian in particular: Ukrainian uses the same alphabet, and Codex searched there. If you have a theory, I'd like to hear it.

The model matters too. Inside the same Claude Code, without help, Haiku passed 3 of 20 runs on Prisma and DeepSeek 18 of 20. Haiku searched in 2 runs of 40, DeepSeek in 10.

Four lines in AGENTS.md closed the gap

These four lines, in English, in every language arm:

When you add or update a dependency:

1. Before you pick a package or a version, run the full `npm view <package>`
   and read `deprecated` and the dist-tags, not only `version`.
2. Check whether the package has moved to a new name.
3. Read the docs that ship inside the package (AGENTS.md, README, type files)
   before the website.
4. Search the web for the official upgrade guide before you change code.

With them, every agent passed every run in every language: Hedera 80 of 80, Prisma 76 of 76. Codex with the Russian task searched in 9 runs of 10, up from 0. Haiku searched in 36 of 40, up from 2. The colleague's note passed everything too.

These lines live in your users' projects, not in your package, and most users won't have them.

The same lines can read your tags differently than you meant

The first version of the Prisma task said "upgrade to the current version", not "version 8". There, the four lines barely helped: 13 of 80 runs. The agents did exactly what the lines asked. They read the dist-tags, saw that prisma@latest is 8.0.0-rc.33, a release candidate, while @prisma/client@latest is still 7.10.1, and most of them wrote in their answer that they were staying on the stable 7.10.1 on purpose. That's a reasonable call. Only the note, which says plainly that current Prisma is 8, got them there.

An agent that reads your dist-tags carefully takes them at their word. If latest points at a release candidate next to a stable 7 on another package, careful agents will choose 7.

What a maintainer can do

A user's agent that skips the search still reads npm, the install output and the package itself. Put the upgrade facts there and they reach users in every language:

  1. Deprecate the old package with a message that names the new one. npm deprecate shows up in the install output and in the full npm view. In Hedera's case npm says nothing, so only a search finds the move.
  2. Ship one last release of the old package whose README says where it moved. The README is what an agent reads after installing it.
  3. Decide what latest means, and keep related packages consistent. A release candidate on latest with the client still on 7 sends careful agents back to 7.
  4. Ship the upgrade note inside the package. Docs in the package were read; docs sites mostly weren't.
  5. Publish a few lines your users can copy into AGENTS.md. The four above, or your own version naming your package. They worked in every language I tried.

The previous article has the measurements behind items 1 to 4.

If you want to see what agents do with your own package, including with tasks in other languages, Ready for Agents runs these checks for library teams.

Limits

Two tasks, both on npm. Five runs per cell, so a single cell says little; the language gap holds across both tasks together, and the four-line result holds in all 32 cells. The Spanish and Ukrainian prompts were machine-translated and checked by two models, not by native speakers. Kimi is missing 9 runs on the Prisma task because of subscription limits. Effort is the default for every agent except Codex (low).

Scripts and the table of every cell: worklore-mcp.

articles.body_html:
You didn't split the class. You hid half of it upstairs

TL;DR: Don't create a superclass just to pass a size limit. Move behavior into collaborators with delegation.

Problems 😔

  • Inheritance without a real specialization
  • Hidden coupling to the superclass
  • Yo-yo navigation across files
  • Fragile base class
  • Vague parent names
  • Responsibilities stay in one object
  • Bijection violation

Solutions 😃

  1. Extract cohesive collaborators
  2. Delegate, don't inherit
  3. Split by responsibility
  4. Name by domain concept
  5. Measure cohesion, not size

Refactorings ⚙️

Refactoring 007 - Extract Class

#webdev #beginners #javascript #tutorial

Context 💬

A harness caps class length, property count, and method count, and it rejects code that goes over.

Some limits work as good alarms for growing responsibilities (long functions, too many attributes, too many methods).

You ask an AI assistant to make the failing class pass.

The shortcut path is moving half of its members into a new parent class.

The count per class drops, the check turns green, and nothing else changes.

The behavior stays in the same object, because the child inherits everything the parent holds.

Developers did this for years to dodge size rules in code reviews.

Now the assistant does it in seconds, and it stacks as many layers as the harness needs.

The parent has no meaning of its own, so it gets names like Base, Part, or Abstract.

You use inheritance to share code, not to model a specialization.

Johnson and Foote suggested factoring shared behavior into abstract superclasses and deep hierarchies back in 1988, and that advice fits frameworks that share real protocols, not size quotas.

The metric improves and the design gets worse.

That's Goodhart's law at work.

Sample Code 💻

Wrong 🚫 

// The harness rejects over 300 lines, 10 attributes or 20 methods.
//
// The agent that tries to prove the Riemann Hypothesis kept
// growing: every new theory and sublemma added methods and
// state to it.
//
// To pass the harness, the assistant moved the overflow
// into superclasses that exist only to hold members.

abstract class ProofBase {
  protected lemmas = new Set<string>();
  protected log: string[] = [];
  // 300 attributes more

  protected record(step: string): void {
    this.log.push(step);
  }

  protected assume(claim: string): void {
    this.lemmas.add(claim);
  }
}

abstract class EulerProductPart extends ProofBase {
  protected eulerProduct(s: number): number {
    this.record(`euler product at ${s}`);
    return 0; // ...
  }

  protected primeCounting(n: number): number {
    return 0; // ...
  }
}

abstract class FunctionalEquationPart extends EulerProductPart {
  protected reflect(s: number): number {
    return 1 - s;
  }

  protected xiSymmetry(s: number): boolean {
    return true; // ...
  }
}

abstract class ZeroSearchPart extends FunctionalEquationPart {
  protected knownZeros: number[] = [];

  protected verifyZerosUpTo(height: number): boolean {
    return true; // ...
  }
}

class RiemannProofAgent extends ZeroSearchPart {
  prove(): boolean {
    this.assume("zeros lie in 0 < Re(s) < 1");
    this.eulerProduct(2.0);
    this.xiSymmetry(0.5);
    return this.verifyZerosUpTo(1e12);
  }

  // 300 methods more
}

Right 👉 

class LemmaLedger {
  private lemmas = new Set<string>();
  private log: string[] = [];

  record(step: string): void {
    this.log.push(step);
  }

  assume(claim: string): void {
    this.lemmas.add(claim);
  }
}

class EulerProduct {
  constructor(private readonly ledger: LemmaLedger) {}

  evaluateAt(s: number): number {
    this.ledger.record(`euler product at ${s}`);
    return 0; // ...
  }

  primeCounting(n: number): number {
    return 0; // ...
  }
}

class FunctionalEquation {
  reflect(s: number): number {
    return 1 - s;
  }

  checkSymmetryAt(s: number): boolean {
    return true; // ...
  }
}

class ZeroVerification {
  private knownZeros: number[] = [];

  verifyUpTo(height: number): boolean {
    return true; // ...
  }
}

class RiemannProofAgent {
  constructor(
    private readonly ledger: LemmaLedger,
    private readonly eulerProduct: EulerProduct,
    private readonly functionalEquation: FunctionalEquation,
    private readonly zeroVerification: ZeroVerification
  ) {}

  prove(): boolean {
    this.ledger.assume("zeros lie in 0 < Re(s) < 1");
    this.eulerProduct.evaluateAt(2.0);
    this.functionalEquation.checkSymmetryAt(0.5);
    return this.zeroVerification.verifyUpTo(1e12);
  }
}

Detection 🔍

[X] Semi-Automatic

Search for abstract classes with a single subclass that no code uses as a type.

If nobody type-hints the parent, it exists only to hold members.

Look for parent names like Base, Part, Helper, or Abstract, and for hierarchies that got deeper right after you introduced a size limit.

Check the history: a failed size check followed by a commit that adds a parent and moves members up is the signature.

Exceptions 🛑

A parent class is fine when several subclasses share a real protocol and callers depend on the parent type.

In that case, the parent models a concept, and you can explain it without mentioning the size limit.

Tags 🏷️

  • Hierarchies

Level 🔋

[x] Intermediate

Why the Bijection Is Important 🗺️

Every class in your model should match a concept in the MAPPER.

A parent class created to hold overflow members matches nothing.

Nobody in the domain would say "this thing is a kind of leftover bucket".

When you delegate to collaborators, each one maps to a concept you can name, and the bijection stays intact.

When you hide members upstairs, the original object keeps every responsibility, and you add coupling between the layers.

AI Generation 🤖

AI generators create this smell often when you ask them to respect a size limit.

They optimize for the check you gave them, and moving members into a parent is the smallest diff that turns it green.

They don't stop to ask whether the new parent models anything.

Humans took this shortcut when they felt the pressure of a review rule, but an assistant takes it on every failing class, without hesitation and without feeling any shame.

AI Detection 🧲

AI can detect it if you point it at the pattern.

Try: "Find abstract classes with a single subclass that no code uses as a type, and explain what concept each one models."

Without that prompt, the hierarchy looks tidy, the harness passes, and most assistants won't flag the code they just wrote.

Try Them! 🛠

Remember: AI Assistants make lots of mistakes

Suggested Prompt: Replace the intermediate superclasses that only hold overflow members with collaborator objects, and delegate to them from the original class

Without Proper Instructions With Specific Instructions
ChatGPT ChatGPT
Claude Claude
Perplexity Perplexity
Copilot Copilot
You You
Gemini Gemini
DeepSeek DeepSeek
Meta AI Meta AI
Grok Grok
Qwen Qwen

Conclusion 🏁

A size limit is an alarm, not a design.

When the alarm rings, split the responsibilities instead of moving them to a parent.

Delegate to small objects you can name, test, and replace.

Don't let the assistant pass the harness by hiding the mess one floor up.

articles.title: I always wanted lyrics floating over my screen while I work, so I built it
articles.description: I love music. It's on all day while I work: a playlist in the background, code in front of me.  And...
articles.body_html:
I love music. It's on all day while I work: a playlist in the background, code in front of me.

And for a long time I've wished for one thing: the lyrics, right there on my screen, on top of whatever I'm doing. Not in another window I have to switch to. Not in a lyrics tab buried behind my editor. Just floating over my work, word by word, in time with the song, so I can sing along without stopping.

So I finally built it.

mondegreen is a free, open-source lyrics overlay for Windows. Play a song in Spotify or YouTube, and the lyrics float on top of every window. Every word lights up the moment it's sung, and everything moves on the beat, so you feel the song instead of just reading it. And when I only want to listen, Ctrl Alt F turns it into a full-screen lyrics visualizer.

(The name: a "mondegreen" is a misheard lyric, like "'scuse me while I kiss this guy." With the real words on screen, those get fixed too.)

nirajkhetre / mondegreen

Free synced lyrics overlay for Spotify on Windows: word-by-word karaoke lyrics on top of your screen, moving with the beat, plus a full-screen lyrics visualizer.

mondegreen: synced lyrics overlay for Spotify on Windows

Word-by-word lyrics that sing along on top of your screen while you work, move with the beat of the song, and turn into a full-screen music visualizer when you just want to listen.

Website · Wiki · Download · Report a bug

A mondegreen is a misheard lyric: "'Scuse me while I kiss this guy." This app is the fix. It shows you the real words, exactly when they're sung.

Why mondegreen

  • Synced to the word, not just the line. Every word lights up the moment it's sung, from word-timed karaoke lyrics, so you never lose your place.
  • It feels the beat. A beat tracker listens to your speakers and locks onto the tempo, so the lyrics bounce, slam and glow on the beat instead of reacting late.
  • Out of your way. A click-through overlay that floats above every window, hides a…
View on GitHub

Getting lyrics on screen was the easy part. Getting them to land exactly when they're sung, and to move on the beat rather than after it, took most of the work. Here's how each piece works.

1. Knowing exactly where the song is

My first version polled the player's position and drifted. Lyrics were a few hundred milliseconds late, then early, then late.

Windows already knows what's playing: the Global System Media Transport Controls session (the media flyout you see when you press a volume key). No Spotify login, no API key, no Premium. I read it from a tiny PowerShell script that prints a JSON line whenever something changes:

$t = $s.GetTimelineProperties()
$o = [ordered]@{
  app = $s.SourceAppUserModelId; title = $meta.Title; artist = $meta.Artist
  pos = [int]$t.Position.TotalMilliseconds; dur = [int]$t.EndTime.TotalMilliseconds
  at = $t.LastUpdatedTime.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()
  playing = ($s.GetPlaybackInfo().PlaybackStatus.ToString() -eq 'Playing')
}

The key is LastUpdatedTime. Each position report carries the player's own timestamp for that position. So between reports I don't guess: the position right now is pos + (now − at).

// the player stamps each position report with its own clock (np.at), so between reports we extrapolate exactly;
// small disagreements glide in instead of jumping, seeks snap
function songPos(now) {
  const np = L.np, target = np.playing ? np.pos + (Date.now() - np.at) : np.pos || 0
  const est = shown + (np.playing ? now - shownAt : 0)
  shown = Math.abs(target - est) > 250 ? target : est + (target - est) * 0.06
  shownAt = now
  return shown - (L.S.delay || 0) + (L.S.offsets?.[L.key] || 0)
}

That one change fixed the drift. On real Spotify songs, vocals came in within 20–200 ms of the line starts. For the songs where a lyric file is off, there's a tap-to-sync shortcut that remembers the offset per song.

One thing I tried and rejected: a native SMTC module for Node. Its lastUpdatedTime came back as the query time, not the player's stamp, which breaks exactly this trick.

2. Lighting up every word

Most synced lyrics are timed per line. I wanted every word.

Kugou's KRC format times every syllable. The files are base64, with a 4-byte header, XOR'd with a fixed 16-byte key, then zlib-compressed. Decoding is four lines in Node:

const raw = Buffer.from(d.content, 'base64').subarray(4)
for (let i = 0; i < raw.length; i++) raw[i] ^= KRC_KEY[i % 16]
const lines = parseKrc(zlib.inflateSync(raw).toString('utf8'), c)
return lines.length > 3 ? { source: 'Kugou', kind: 'word', lines } : null

When Kugou has nothing, LRCLIB is the fallback, with line timing; I spread the words across each line by syllable count so they still light up one by one.

The rule that saved me from the most wrong lyrics: both sources must match the track's length (within 3–4 seconds). A live version or an extended mix never gets studio timing. YouTube titles like Artist - Song (Official Video) [4K] get cleaned up before searching, and everything is cached on disk, so a song you've played before shows its lyrics instantly, even offline.

3. Hearing the beat before it lands

Reacting to the beat isn't enough. By the time you detect a kick, it's already over, so anything you animate is late. I wanted the page to know when the next beat lands.

Everything runs in an AudioWorklet on the audio thread, fed by system-audio loopback:

  1. Onset envelope. Split the audio into low, mid and high bands and keep the rises in energy (spectral flux), about 94 frames a second.
  2. Tempo. Autocorrelate the last 8 seconds of that envelope. Peaks are candidate beat periods; a soft preference for ~120 BPM stops it from picking half or double the real tempo: 
const bpm = 60 * fps / L, s = r[L] * Math.exp(-0.5 * (Math.log2(bpm / 120) / 0.8) ** 2)
  1. Hold the grid. The hardest bug: on some songs it kept flipping between half and double the real tempo, and the whole scene jittered. Half, double and 2:3 tempos are the same groove heard differently, so they never reset the grid. A genuinely new tempo has to win four checks in a row: 
else if (![0.5, 2 / 3, 1.5, 2].some(h => Math.abs(ratio / h - 1) < 0.045) && candConf > 0.35) {
  if (this.streak && Math.abs(cand / this.challenger - 1) < 0.04) this.streak++
  else { this.challenger = cand; this.streak = 1 }
  if (this.streak >= 4) { this.period = cand; this.anchor = 0; this.streak = 0 }
}
  1. Phase lock. Find the offset where the last ~4 seconds of onsets pile up, then nudge the grid halfway toward it on each check, like a phase-locked loop with a gain of 0.5.

With that, the grid error on real songs dropped to 0–9 ms. Animations are scheduled for the predicted beat, so they land on it. When there's no steady tempo (intros, ballads), confidence drops and the visuals react to hits instead.

4. What a 144 Hz screen did to my CPU

The first build used CSS animations everywhere. On my laptop's 144 Hz screen, every one of them ran 144 times a second, inside a transparent always-on-top window, which costs a full copy per frame. The overlay sat at up to 127% of a core; the settings window, with its live previews, hit 275%.

The fix: no CSS animations or filters on anything that moves. One loop drives all motion by setting a few CSS variables per word, capped at 60 fps (or 30), sleeping with setTimeout and only then asking for a frame:

// sleep until the next frame is due, then ask for a frame (asking every vsync would wake us 144 times a second)
if (f.paused) timer = setTimeout(() => loop(performance.now()), 100)
else timer = setTimeout(() => { timer = 0; raf = requestAnimationFrame(loop) }, Math.max(0, FRAME - (performance.now() - drawn) - 6))

The overlay dropped to 40–70% of one core while animating, about 6% hidden. Settings went from 275% to about 85%, mostly by letting preview cards animate only under the mouse.

5. Twelve looks and ten full-screen scenes

Since every look reads the same word timings and beat clock, adding looks became fun: a notch that stretches to each line, a split-flap departures board, a ransom-note zine, words that fall and bounce on the beat. There are twelve.

Listen mode (Ctrl Alt F) runs one WebGL2 fragment shader per scene, driven by a monotonic beat counter instead of time, so lasers jump on beats and suns step down per beat. Each scene is coloured from the album art.

My favourite, Late Night Texts, has no image files at all. It's an SVG drawn in code to look like a sketchbook: feTurbulence plus feDisplacementMap wobble every ink line, a noise mask makes them grainy like pencil, and the watercolour washes are blurred, displaced fills with mix-blend-mode: multiply.

<filter id="sk-ink">
  <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency=".03" numOctaves="2" seed="3" result="n"/>
  <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="n" scale="3.4" xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G"/>
</filter>

The guy never moves; the room does. Sound lines leave his headphones on each beat, and the lyrics arrive as a chat on his monitor. The effect lines re-roll their wobble every few frames, which reads as hand-drawn "line boil".

6. Shipping a Windows exe

electron-builder makes the installer and a portable exe. One gotcha to plan for: PowerShell can't read files inside the app.asar archive, so the now-playing script would fail in the packaged app. The fix is to ship the scripts unpacked and point at that folder:

"asarUnpack": ["*.ps1"]

const scripts = __dirname.replace(/app\.asar$/, 'app.asar.unpacked')

What I'd do next

  • Code-sign the exe, so SmartScreen stops warning on first run.
  • Show translation lines (KRC files already carry them).
  • Calibrate Bluetooth latency automatically from the loopback audio.

Try it

It's free and MIT-licensed. Windows 10 or 11, installer or portable exe:

  • Download: https://github.com/nirajkhetre/mondegreen/releases/latest
  • Wiki (deep dives): https://github.com/nirajkhetre/mondegreen/wiki

articles.title: CORS with Cookies Between Next.js and a NestJS API: Preflights, Credentials, and When to Proxy Instead — Field Notes
articles.description: Headline: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule that decides whether page...
articles.body_html:
Headline: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule that decides whether page JavaScript may read a response from another origin; it does not stop the request from reaching your server. For a Next.js frontend calling a NestJS API with cookies, either return the exact origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and a 2xx preflight, or proxy /api through a Next.js rewrite so the browser never makes a cross-origin call.

Every project where I split a Next.js frontend from a NestJS API hits the same three CORS errors, in order: the preflight fails, the wildcard origin is rejected once cookies are involved, and then every call returns 200 while the user stays logged out because the session cookie never travels. Here is what each failure means and the setup I ended up with.

Key takeaways

  • CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server: it controls whether page JavaScript can read a cross-origin response, and it does not stop the request from reaching your API.
  • A JSON Content-Type, an Authorization header, or a PUT/PATCH/DELETE method makes a request non-simple, so the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight — without cookies — and needs a 2xx response with matching allow headers.
  • Credentialed requests (credentials: 'include') require Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true plus the exact requesting origin; Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is rejected.
  • Cookies cross origins only when the request opts in and SameSite allows it; across different sites that means SameSite=None; Secure, which Safari's default third-party cookie blocking still defeats.
  • Proxying /api/* through a Next.js rewrite makes the API same-origin: no preflights and first-party cookies, at the cost of one extra network hop.

What does CORS actually protect?

CORS protects the user's data inside the browser, not your server. An origin is the combination of scheme, host, and port, so https://app.example.com and https://api.example.com are different origins. The same-origin policy stops a page on one origin from reading responses from another, and CORS response headers are how a server opts specific origins back in.

Three consequences took me too long to internalize:

  • Only browsers enforce CORS. curl, Postman, a Next.js Server Component, and a NestJS service calling another service never send preflights or check Access-Control-* headers.
  • A blocked request may still have run. For a simple cross-origin request, the browser sends it, the server executes it, and only the response is hidden from JavaScript.
  • CORS is not CSRF protection. A forged form POST from another site still reaches the API with whatever cookies the browser attaches; SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, or an Origin header check are what stop it.

Same-origin and same-site are different tests, and cookies follow the same-site test. A site is the scheme plus the registrable domain (eTLD+1, such as example.com), and ports do not count:

Request from Request to Same-origin? Same-site?
https://app.example.com https://api.example.com No — host differs Yes — both on example.com
http://localhost:3000 http://localhost:4000 No — port differs Yes — ports do not count
https://shop.vercel.app https://shop-api.vercel.app No No — vercel.app is a public suffix

Why does my fetch trigger a preflight OPTIONS request?

The browser sends an OPTIONS preflight before any cross-origin request that is not "simple". A simple request uses GET, HEAD, or POST, sets only CORS-safelisted headers, and sends a Content-Type of text/plain, multipart/form-data, or application/x-www-form-urlencoded. A JSON body, an Authorization header, a custom header such as Idempotency-Key, or a PUT, PATCH, or DELETE method each force a preflight, so almost every real API call gets one:

await fetch('https://api.example.com/api/orders', {
  method: 'POST',
  credentials: 'include', // send and store cookies cross-origin
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, // not simple → preflight
  body: JSON.stringify(order),
});

The preflight announces the method and headers in Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server must answer with a 2xx status plus Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, and Access-Control-Allow-Headers values that cover them. Preflight requests never carry cookies or an Authorization header. My first failure came from exactly that rule: an auth middleware registered with app.use() above app.enableCors() answered every preflight with 401, and the browser reported it as a CORS error.

Access-Control-Max-Age sets how long the browser caches a preflight result. Without the header, the Fetch spec default is 5 seconds; Chromium caps the value at 7200 seconds and Firefox at 86400 seconds.

Why can't I use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with cookies?

A credentialed request — fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' }) or XMLHttpRequest.withCredentials = true — is readable only when the response sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and an Access-Control-Allow-Origin equal to the requesting origin. Chrome rejects the wildcard with: "The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header in the response must not be the wildcard '' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'." For credentialed requests, a ` in Access-Control-Allow-Headers, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, or Access-Control-Expose-Headers` is treated as a literal name, not a wildcard.

The tempting fix is to reflect whatever Origin arrives — origin: true in the cors package that NestJS uses with the Express adapter. Combined with credentials: true, reflection lets any website read authenticated responses for a logged-in user. I use an exact allowlist from an environment variable instead:

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

const allowedOrigins = new Set(
  (process.env.CORS_ORIGIN ?? '').split(',').map((o) => o.trim()).filter(Boolean),
);

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.enableCors({
    origin: (origin, callback) => {
      // No Origin header: curl, server-to-server calls — CORS does not apply
      if (!origin || allowedOrigins.has(origin)) return callback(null, true);
      callback(null, false); // omit CORS headers; the browser blocks the read
    },
    credentials: true, // Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
    methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
    allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization', 'Idempotency-Key'],
    exposedHeaders: ['ETag', 'X-Request-Id'],
    maxAge: 7200, // Chromium's cap for preflight caching
  });
  await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
}
void bootstrap();

The details in that config that matter:

  • callback(null, false), not an Error. Returning false omits the CORS headers and lets the browser block the read; passing an Error turns the request into a 500 under Express.
  • Exact strings only. A suffix regex like /example\.com$/ also matches https://evil-example.com, and allowlisting null admits every sandboxed iframe and file:// page, because those send Origin: null.
  • Vary: Origin on every reflected response. The cors package adds it automatically; a hand-written middleware must add it too, or a CDN can serve one origin's Access-Control-Allow-Origin to another.
  • Response headers are opt-in. JavaScript can read only CORS-safelisted response headers such as Content-Type; ETag and X-Request-Id stay invisible until listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

Why are my cookies not sent on cross-origin requests?

A cookie crosses origins only when three layers agree: the request opts in, the cookie's SameSite attribute allows the context, and the browser's third-party cookie policy allows it. fetch() defaults to credentials: 'same-origin', so a cross-origin call needs credentials: 'include' before the browser sends any cookie or stores any Set-Cookie from the response.

When the frontend and API share a site — app.example.com and api.example.com — the request is same-site, and SameSite=Lax cookies are sent. Chrome treats a cookie with no SameSite attribute as Lax. A cookie set by api.example.com without a Domain attribute is host-only, so Next.js middleware on app.example.com cannot read it; Domain=example.com shares it with both hosts.

When they are different sites — such as two *.vercel.app deployments, because vercel.app is on the Public Suffix List — the session cookie becomes a third-party cookie. It needs SameSite=None; Secure, and even then Safari blocks third-party cookies by default and Chrome blocks them in Incognito. I stopped shipping cross-site cookie auth: either the API moves to a subdomain of the frontend's site, or the frontend proxies it.

When should I proxy API calls through a Next.js rewrite instead of enabling CORS?

Proxy through a Next.js rewrite when one frontend owns the API; keep CORS when several origins, a mobile app, or third parties call the API directly. A rewrite lets the browser call /api/... on its own origin while the Next.js server forwards the request to the backend, so there is no preflight, no CORS header, and every cookie is first-party:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  async rewrites() {
    return [
      {
        source: '/api/:path*',
        destination: `${process.env.API_URL}/api/:path*`,
      },
    ];
  },
};

export default nextConfig;

The browser now calls fetch('/api/me') with the default credentials: 'same-origin'. A rewrites array runs after Next.js checks its own routes, so a local app/api route handler with the same path still wins. Two backend changes came with the switch: session cookies must be host-only, because the browser rejects Domain=api.example.com on the frontend's host; and rate limiting or logging must read the client IP from X-Forwarded-For instead of the socket address.

Direct CORS Next.js rewrite proxy
Preflight On every non-simple request, cached up to Access-Control-Max-Age None — requests are same-origin
Cookies Need credentials: 'include'; cross-site needs SameSite=None; Secure and fails under third-party cookie blocking First-party; SameSite=Lax works
Network path Browser → API Browser → Next.js → API (one extra hop)
Configuration Origin allowlist on the API for every environment One API_URL variable on the frontend

Why does a 500 error show up as a CORS error?

A failed response without Access-Control-Allow-Origin is reported as a CORS error, which hides the real status code. JavaScript receives only a generic TypeError — "Failed to fetch" in Chrome — with no status. The usual causes are an error handler or gateway that responds before the CORS middleware runs, and nginx: add_header applies only to 2xx and 3xx responses unless the directive ends with always.

When a CORS error appears, I check the Network tab for the real status first, then replay the preflight with curl:

# Replay the preflight a browser would send
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/api/orders \
  -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type'

A correct response returns 204 with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, and an Access-Control-Allow-Headers value that includes content-type. If those headers are missing, the fix belongs on the server or the proxy, not in the frontend fetch() call.

FAQ

Q: Why does my API work in Postman or curl but fail in the browser?

A: CORS is enforced only by browsers. curl and Postman never send preflights or check Access-Control-* headers, so a missing or wrong CORS configuration shows up only when page JavaScript calls the API.

Q: Does mode: 'no-cors' fix a CORS error?

A: No. mode: 'no-cors' returns an opaque response with status 0 and an unreadable body, and it allows only simple requests. It silences the error by hiding the data.

Q: Is CORS a CSRF protection?

A: No. Simple cross-origin requests, such as an HTML form POST, still reach the server with cookies attached; CORS only stops the attacker's page from reading the response. Use SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, or an Origin header check against CSRF.
