articles.title: Treat LLM Output as a Build Artifact: Batch APIs and Jev
articles.description: How precomputing every answer turned a 31-second request into a 2 KB static file, with a frontier...
articles.body_html:
How precomputing every answer turned a 31-second request into a 2 KB static file, with a frontier model writing and Jev checking its work.

A model call per request is the wrong default

The first version of the demo took 31 seconds to answer a single click.

It was a personalization demo. A visitor picks any of 12 interests and gets a short paragraph describing people who share them. Behind each click, the server made 11 data calls and 7 model calls while the visitor watched a spinner. A cache wouldn't have saved it either, because a cache only helps the second person to pick the same selection.


Somewhere around call 14, the visitor grew a beard.

Then I did the arithmetic. Twelve interests give 2¹² − 1 = 4,095 possible selections. That's few enough to write every answer before anyone asks.

That turns the model's output into a build artifact. A build step generates and checks every paragraph offline and writes each one to a static file. The model runs once, at build time, the way a compiler does.

The examples below use a made-up online shop instead of the original project. It has 12 filters such as "waterproof" and "vegan materials", which gives 4,095 filter combinations, and each combination gets a short "who buys this" paragraph grounded in the shop's own product attributes and reviews.

The approach rests on two ideas: precompute the whole space, and split the work between two models. A frontier model writes, and Jev checks what it wrote. Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13) is a small decision model from TypeSafe, available through OpenRouter. It returns typed answers with confidences instead of free text. The writer's calls go through a batch API at half price, behind a small queue that keeps the code as simple as a normal await.

Precompute the whole space

The page never talks to a model. It fetches a file that the build step wrote earlier, one per combination.

Each selection is encoded as a bit field, where filter n sets bit n. The result is a number from 1 to 4,095 that also names the file.

const mask = selected
  .reduce((m, i) => m | (1 << i), 0);
const res = await fetch(
  `/api/writeup/${mask}.json`);

A file is about 2 KB and a CDN serves it in milliseconds. Nothing in the request path needs an API key or can hit a rate limit, and the bill doesn't grow with traffic.

Building ahead of time has a second benefit: every output can be checked before a visitor sees it. You can't do that when the model writes at request time. The cost is paid once, during the build.

This only works while the space stays countable. Twelve inputs give 4,095 combinations, while twenty would give more than a million. Past some size, one full pass stops being affordable.

To ship before the run finishes, sort the work queue by how close each combination is to the default selection. The combinations a visitor reaches in one or two clicks are done first and can be published while the rest of the run continues.

Every sentence traces to evidence

With the model out of the request path, there is time to check its work. The pipeline uses that time so that every sentence a shopper reads can be traced back to data.

Each combination goes through nine steps.

  1. Evidence. Pull structured signals from the shop's data, both for the whole combination and for each filter on its own. Each signal is credited to the filters that drive it and gets a row number such as E7.
  2. Claims. The writer proposes 4 claims that cite evidence rows by id. Each must stay under 20 words and avoid explanatory clauses.
  3. Rule checks. Plain code drops any claim that cites a row that doesn't exist or names a forbidden term.
  4. Fact-check. Jev gets one request per combination with one question per claim, and labels each claim supported, overstated or unsupported. A claim survives only as "supported" with a confidence of at least 0.6. Because Jev can't rewrite anything, a weak claim is dropped.
  5. Repair. When a filter has no surviving claim, the writer proposes one claim for it, and that claim goes through steps 3 and 4.
  6. Paragraph. The writer turns the kept claims into 3 to 4 sentences and tags each claim's phrase.
  7. Faithfulness. Jev estimates the probability that the paragraph adds a fact none of the claims contain. At 0.5 or higher the writer rewrites the paragraph, up to 3 times.
  8. Retry. If too few claims survive, the model steps run again with fresh answers, up to 6 attempts per combination.
  9. Ship. The build writes one JSON file per combination.

A claim stays short and plain so that it can be checked against its rows.

{
  "id": "C1",
  "text": "Shop for wet daily commutes",
  "evidence": ["E3", "E7"]
}

In the paragraph, a tag marks the phrase that came from each claim.

These shoppers <b c="C1">walk to
work in the rain</b> and ...

The page uses that tag to show the evidence behind each phrase, so hovering over "walk to work in the rain" shows rows E3 and E7. A reader can check the paragraph without having to trust it.

This is a real claim from the project: "In restaurants and venues, they gravitate toward cozy, romantic, intimate settings." Its evidence rows are below.

{
  "id": "C1",
  "evidence": [
    { "name": "Cozy", "category": "Places", "score": 0.98 },
    { "name": "Romantic", "category": "Places", "score": 0.96 },
    { "name": "Intimate", "category": "Places", "score": 0.89 }
  ]
}

Splitting the work this way keeps each check narrow. A claim is judged on its own against the rows it names, and the paragraph is judged only on whether it adds anything, so a small model like Jev can handle both questions.

A frontier model writes, Jev checks

To cut costs, I first used a smaller model as the writer. It kept adding explanations nobody asked for, such as "favoring calm, considered design over clutter", and Jev correctly called them overstated. Only 25% of its claims survived.

That failure led to the rule limiting claims to 20 words without explanatory clauses, which raised survival to 52%. The paragraphs built from the survivors still read badly, though, with invented details and stilted boilerplate that the checks flagged but couldn't fix.

So I went back to a frontier model, Claude Opus, for the writing. Writing is open-ended, and its quality shows in every sentence. Judging is a closed question about one claim and the few rows behind it, and a small model handles that well.


The writer gets the budget. The checker gets the red pen.

Jev doesn't take a free-form prompt. It takes a state object plus named questions and returns a typed answer for each. A choice question returns an option with a confidence, and a noul question returns the probability of yes.

The criteria are plain text, defined once.

const criteria = {
  supported:
    'Every quality the claim names comes ' +
    'from its evidence, in plain words. ' +
    'Naming two signals together is supported.',
  overstated:
    'Adds something no evidence names: a ' +
    'detail, an absolute degree, a motive, ' +
    'or one new kind of item that merges ' +
    'separate signals.',
  unsupported:
    'The evidence does not point this way.',
};

One request then checks every claim in a combination.

const state = { items: claims.map((cl) =>
  ({ claim: cl.text, evidence: cl.evidence })) };

const questions = Object.fromEntries(
  claims.map((_, i) => [`c${i}`, {
    type: 'choice',
    instructions: `Judge items[${i}].claim ` +
      `against only items[${i}].evidence.`,
    criteria,
  }]));

const { answers } = await post(
  'https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions',
  { model: 'typesafe/jev-1.13',
    state, questions });

Since the answers come back typed, keeping a claim is a plain filter.

const kept = claims.filter((_, i) => {
  const a = answers[`c${i}`];
  return a?.choice === 'supported'
    && a.confidence >= 0.6;
});

Faithfulness uses a single noul question named added, and the writer rewrites the paragraph when its probability is 0.5 or higher. I set that threshold low because a rewrite costs little and padding that reaches a reader costs more.

Across the final run, all of Jev's checks for 4,077 combinations cost $0.42. Not per combination. In total.

Test Jev before you trust it

Before Jev saw real work, I gave it cases with known answers. It labeled a supported, a deliberately overstated and an unsupported claim correctly, at confidences of 0.89, 1.00 and 0.82. It scored a faithful paragraph 0.18 for added facts and a paragraph with invented facts 0.97, and it agreed with the frontier model on 17 of the 18 claims that model had already approved.

That's a small smoke test: 3 claims, 2 paragraphs and 18 cross-checked claims. It gave me enough confidence to start the run, and the run itself showed what it missed.

The last 18 combinations kept failing. In one of them, the claim "drawn to detective work and corruption" rested on two evidence rows naming exactly those signals at maximum strength, and Jev still called it overstated with confidence up to 0.94.


Jev, confidently wrong about a correct claim.

Jev had read the two signals, named together, as one new thing merged from both. My first criteria never said that naming them together was allowed. So I rewrote the criteria: naming signals together is supported, and only merging them into a single new kind of item is overstated. Those are the two sentences you saw in the criteria above.

With the new wording, the misjudged claims passed at 0.84 to 0.97, while real overstatements still failed at 0.95 to 0.99. At the same time I raised the keep threshold from 0.5 to 0.6. The main run had used 0.5 with the first wording, and the new settings applied to the last 8 combinations.

Criteria for a decision model deserve the same care as code. I now keep a set of known cases, rerun it after every wording change, and read whatever still fails. When a run stalls on the same few inputs, check the criteria before you blame the writer.

Half-price batches you can await

Model providers offer a batch API at about half price, where you upload many requests at once and download the results when the batch finishes. Pipelines written around that shape end up as a submit-and-poll loop that matches results back to requests, which is hard to read and harder to change.

A small queue avoids that by letting pipeline code call batched(params) and await it like a normal request. Behind it, calls collect until 20 seconds pass with no new ones or 2,000 are waiting, and then go out as one batch.


Half fare, as long as you don't mind waiting for the bus.

const queue = [];
let idle = null, nextId = 0;

export const batched = (params) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    enqueue({ id: `r${nextId++}`, params,
      resolve, reject, tries: 0 }));

function enqueue(it) {
  queue.push(it);
  if (queue.length >= 2000) return flush();
  clearTimeout(idle);
  idle = setTimeout(flush, 20_000);
}

function flush() {
  clearTimeout(idle); idle = null;
  const items = queue.splice(0);
  if (items.length) runBatch(items);
}

runBatch submits the batch and settles each waiting promise once the batch ends.

async function runBatch(items) {
  const b = await client.messages.batches
    .create({ requests: items.map((it) =>
      ({ custom_id: it.id, params: it.params })) });
  await waitUntilEnded(b.id); // poll every 30s
  const byId = new Map(
    items.map((it) => [it.id, it]));
  const results = await client.messages
    .batches.results(b.id);
  for await (const r of results) {
    const it = byId.get(r.custom_id);
    byId.delete(r.custom_id);
    if (r.result.type === 'succeeded')
      it.resolve(r.result.message);
    else retryOrReject(it, r.result.type);
  }
  for (const it of byId.values())
    it.reject(new Error('missing'));
}

retryOrReject puts a failed or expired request back in the queue up to twice and then rejects it. In real code, wrap the body in a try/catch that rejects every item if the batch itself fails.

The queue pays off only when many calls are waiting at the same moment, so the build starts all 4,095 combinations at once. Each one runs until its first await, which puts every claims call into the first round of batches. The 2,000 cap splits that round across a few batches, and after Jev filters the claims, every paragraph call fills the next round. The whole run took 12 batches, and the pipeline code still reads like sequential code.

The trade-off: batching makes the run take longer without adding any calls, because each combination waits on several batch rounds.

A cache keyed on the exact request

A disk cache makes iteration cheap. Every external response is stored under a key built from the exact request.

async function cached(key, fn) {
  const file = path.join(
    CACHE, sha256(key) + '.json');
  if (fs.existsSync(file))
    return JSON.parse(
      fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8'));
  const value = await fn();
  fs.writeFileSync(file, JSON.stringify(value));
  return value;
}

const llm = (params, attempt = 0) => cached(
  `llm|${JSON.stringify(params)}|${attempt}`,
  () => batched(params));

Because finished calls are cache hits, a stopped run resumes for free. Changing one prompt changes only that step's keys, so only that step and the steps after it run again. A retry passes its attempt number into the key to get a fresh answer instead of the cached one.

The numbers

The shipped setup cost about $0.03 per combination, a quarter of the first setup.

The first setup used a frontier model for both writing and judging, at full price, and cost about $0.12 per combination, or about $490 projected for all 4,095. The cheaper writer with batching and Jev cost $0.017 to $0.02 per combination, but its paragraphs weren't good enough to ship.

These are the figures for the final run.

  • Combinations finished in the main run: 4,077 of 4,095
  • Cost: $120.66
  • Batches: 12
  • Wall time: about 53 minutes
  • All Jev checks: $0.42

The last 18 finished later for about $1.20 more, 10 through retries and 8 after the criteria fix, so all 4,095 shipped.

I didn't measure how much of the roughly 4x saving came from batching and how much from moving the checks to Jev. The writer model was the same in the first and shipped setups, so the difference comes from those two changes alone. Batching halves the price of every model call, and Jev's total bill was $0.42.

A visitor now downloads one static file of about 2 KB per selection. The first version took 31 seconds per request.

Where else this works

The pattern fits any feature whose inputs can be listed and whose output can wait for a build. Some examples:

  • quiz results for each answer pattern
  • onboarding paths for each combination of role and goal
  • product copy for each variant
  • localized copy for each string and language
  • support answers for known issue types
  • landing pages for each city or category

It's worth doing when you can list every input and afford one pass over all of them. Then the checking pipeline lets you review every output before it ships, which request-time generation never allows.

Before you reach for a faster model or a bigger cache, count the inputs. If the number fits in a build, the visitor never has to wait for a model at all.

Further reading

Jev

  • Jev on OpenRouter. The developer guide covers the Decisions API endpoint used in this article and the three question types: choice, noul and score. Input costs $0.042 per million tokens, and output tokens are free.
  • Introducing System One models and Jev. TypeSafe's launch post explains the model class Jev belongs to, built to return structured decisions that software can use directly.

Batch APIs

Most providers sell batch processing at half price. The queue above works with any of them.

  • Anthropic Message Batches. Usage is billed at 50% of standard prices. A batch holds up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, and most batches finish within an hour. The code in this article uses its create and results calls.
  • OpenAI Batch API. Costs 50% less than the standard API, has its own higher rate limits and turns jobs around within 24 hours. Requests go in a JSONL file uploaded through the Files API, so the queue would write a file instead of an array.
  • Fireworks Batch API. Serverless prices are halved for open-weight and custom models. Input is a JSONL dataset of up to 80 GiB. Jobs expire after a period you choose between 12 and 72 hours. An expired job can be continued so that only its unfinished requests run again.
  • Gemini Batch API. Asynchronous bulk jobs cost 50% of standard pricing. Google also offers Flex inference at the same discount for synchronous calls, which gives you a cheap awaitable call without writing a queue.

Originally published on Medium.

Have you shipped LLM output as a build artifact, or does it still run at request time for you? I'd like to hear where this pattern breaks.

articles.title: Why Google Forms Autofill Extensions Break on Modern Dropdowns (And How I Fixed It in Chrome MV3)
articles.description: If you test multi-page Google Forms for QA, or fill out the same intake/feedback forms repeatedly,...
articles.body_html:
If you test multi-page Google Forms for QA, or fill out the same intake/feedback forms repeatedly, you have probably noticed that most popular autofill extensions on the Chrome Web Store silently skip dropdowns, clear answers between pages, or fail on grid questions.

I ran into the same issues and ended up building Form Deck — a Manifest V3 Chrome extension that runs 100% locally in the browser. Here is what actually breaks under the hood on modern Google Forms DOMs and how I fixed it.

1. input.value = "..." Does Not Update Google's Internal Wiz State

Google Forms uses Google's Wiz framework, which tracks field state via event listeners rather than reading raw DOM .value attributes on submit or page navigation. If an extension simply sets el.value = "Alex", the text appears visually, then disappears or fails required validation when you click Next.

The reliable fix is invoking the native prototype descriptor setter, focusing the element, and dispatching input, change, and blur events with { bubbles: true }:

function setNativeValue(el, value) {
  if (!el) return;
  const str = String(value == null ? '' : value);
  try { el.focus({ preventScroll: true }); } catch { el.focus(); }

  const proto = el.tagName === 'TEXTAREA'
    ? HTMLTextAreaElement.prototype
    : HTMLInputElement.prototype;
  const desc = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(proto, 'value');
  if (desc && typeof desc.set === 'function') {
    desc.set.call(el, str);
  } else {
    el.value = str;
  }

  el.dispatchEvent(new Event('input', { bubbles: true }));
  el.dispatchEvent(new Event('change', { bubbles: true }));
  el.dispatchEvent(new Event('blur', { bubbles: true }));
}

2. role="listbox" Dropdowns Render Options Asynchronously

Unlike a standard HTML <select>, a Google Forms dropdown is a role="listbox" widget. Before you click it, its visible role="option" nodes either are not mounted or live inside closed listboxes elsewhere on the page. When clicked, the menu options appear asynchronously—sometimes inside an expanded listbox and sometimes inside a portal menu.

Clicking synchronously and immediately querying options fails almost every time. Instead, Form Deck snapshots already-visible options before tapping the trigger, simulates a full pointer+mouse tap sequence, and polls briefly until newly revealed selectable options appear:

async function selectFromListbox(listbox, targetText) {
  const currentSelected = listbox.querySelector('[role="option"][aria-selected="true"]');
  if (currentSelected && optionMatchesValue(currentSelected.textContent, targetText)) {
    return true;
  }

  const preVisible = new Set(
    Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('[role="option"]')).filter(isVisible)
  );
  listbox.scrollIntoView({ block: 'center', behavior: 'instant' });
  const trigger = listbox.querySelector('[jsname="LgbsSe"], .ry3kXd, [aria-haspopup="listbox"]') || listbox;
  simulateTap(trigger);
  if (trigger !== listbox) simulateTap(listbox);

  const deadline = Date.now() + 1600;
  while (Date.now() < deadline) {
    const visibleOpts = findOpenDropdownOptions(listbox, preVisible);
    const labelOf = (o) => o.getAttribute('aria-label') || o.getAttribute('data-value') || o.textContent;
    const matchNow = findBestMatchingOption(visibleOpts, targetText, labelOf);
    if (matchNow) {
      simulateTap(matchNow);
      await sleep(140);
      return true;
    }
    await sleep(50);
  }

  document.dispatchEvent(new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'Escape', code: 'Escape', bubbles: true }));
  await sleep(60);
  return false;
}

A few edge cases that also matter in practice:

  • Placeholder skipping: ignore disabled options or empty data-value items labeled Choose / Select / Chọn.
  • Fallback matching tiers: match exact normalized text first, then word-boundary match, then substring match so slight wording changes don't break rules.
  • __other_option__ choices: radio and checkbox groups with an "Other" fill-in box carry data-value="__other_option__"—selecting the choice must wait briefly and then call setNativeValue on the adjacent text input.

3. Split Date/Time Widgets, Grids & Multi-Page Capture

Modern Google Forms also vary by locale and question type:

  • Date & Time widgets may render as HTML5 type="date" / type="time" or split aria-label inputs (Month/Day/Year, Hour/Minute, plus an AM/PM role="listbox", or localized labels like Tháng/Ngày/Năm, Giờ/Phút).
  • Multiple-choice & Checkbox grids pack multiple [role="radiogroup"] or [role="group"] rows inside one div[role="listitem"], often with aria-label strings like "RowName, response for ColumnName".
  • Multi-page forms unmount Page 1 when you click Next. Capturing answers keyed by stable data-item-id (with normalized question title as fallback) lets you replay Page 1, Page 2, and Page 3 reliably after editing a form.

4. Minimal Permissions & Zero-Server Privacy

Because autofill touches names, emails, and test data, I kept the MV3 manifest.json strictly minimal:

"permissions": ["storage", "activeTab"],
"content_scripts": [{
  "matches": ["https://docs.google.com/forms/*"],
  "run_at": "document_idle"
}]
  • All profiles, saved forms, custom regex/keyword rules, and CSV batch rows stay in chrome.storage.local—zero backend calls, zero analytics, zero telemetry.
  • The floating Quick Dock (Alt+Shift+F) renders inside a Shadow DOM root so Google Forms CSS never collides with the UI.

Try It Free (Feedback Welcome!)

For the v1.0.0 release, every feature — unlimited local profiles, 1-click Form Capture, QA Random Fill (populates required text, scales, and grids in <1s), and the CSV Batch Runner — is 100% free with no account required.

  • Try the interactive browser simulator (no install needed): formdeck.pages.dev/qa-testing
  • Install from Chrome Web Store: Form Deck — Multi-Profile Autofill for Google Forms

If you run into a tricky Google Forms layout, localized date picker, or custom grid that trips up autofill extensions, drop a comment below and I will test and fix it in the next release!

articles.title: Test Email Address Deliverability in Node.js: MX Records, Null MX and the Retry Trap
articles.description: Picture it: Black Friday weekend, your signup form is on fire, and somewhere in the flood is...
articles.body_html:
Picture it: Black Friday weekend, your signup form is on fire, and somewhere in the flood is jane@gmial.com. Your app cheerfully fires off a welcome email, a receipt and a password reset to a domain that has never received a message in its life. Each one bounces. Multiply that by a busy weekend and your sending reputation starts to look like a fridge after Thanksgiving: technically still working, but nobody's proud of it.

The fix starts before you send. If you want to test email address deliverability at signup, the cheapest, most honest check is DNS: does this domain actually say it accepts mail? This post builds that check in Node.js with zero dependencies, following the rules the mail RFCs actually set, and is upfront about what DNS can't tell you.

What a DNS check can (and can't) tell you

A DNS check answers one question well: can mail for this domain be delivered anywhere at all? It catches typo domains, dead domains, and domains that explicitly refuse mail.

It does not tell you whether the mailbox jane exists. Only the receiving server knows that, and it may not tell you. Probing it with an SMTP RCPT TO from your app server is a trap: plenty of servers accept every address and bounce later, some greylist you, and repeated probing from one IP looks a lot like address harvesting. Leave mailbox-level verification to a double opt-in email, which also proves the person wanted to hear from you.

The rules, straight from the RFCs

Three rules decide what your code should do:

  1. MX first. RFC 5321, section 5.1: look up MX records for the domain. If the lookup says the domain doesn't exist, that "MUST be reported as an error". If you get a temporary error, the message "MUST be queued and retried later". So a DNS timeout is not a reason to reject a signup.
  2. No MX? Use the implicit MX. Same section: if the MX list comes back empty, the address is treated as if it had an implicit MX pointing at the domain itself. A domain with only an A or AAAA record can still receive mail.
  3. Null MX means "no mail, ever". RFC 7505 defines a single MX record with preference 0 and an exchange of . as the way a domain says it does not accept email. A domain that publishes it must not publish any other MX.

And two length limits from RFC 5321, section 4.5.3.1: the local part (before the @) is at most 64 octets, and a domain at most 255.

The code (about 50 lines, no dependencies) 

import { promises as dns } from "node:dns";

// Deliberately loose: the goal is to catch obvious junk, not to re-implement RFC 5322.
const SYNTAX = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/;

// Errors that mean "ask again later", not "this address is dead".
const TEMPORARY = new Set(["ETIMEOUT", "ESERVFAIL", "ECONNREFUSED", "EAI_AGAIN"]);

export async function checkAddress(address, resolver = dns) {
  const verdict = (status, reason, extra = {}) => ({ address, status, reason, ...extra });

  if (!SYNTAX.test(address)) return verdict("reject", "bad-syntax");

  const at = address.lastIndexOf("@");
  const local = address.slice(0, at);
  const domain = address.slice(at + 1).toLowerCase().replace(/\.$/, "");

  // RFC 5321 4.5.3.1: local-part max 64 octets, domain max 255 octets.
  if (Buffer.byteLength(local) > 64) return verdict("reject", "local-part-too-long");
  if (Buffer.byteLength(domain) > 255) return verdict("reject", "domain-too-long");

  let mx = [];
  try {
    mx = await resolver.resolveMx(domain);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.code === "ENOTFOUND") return verdict("reject", "domain-does-not-exist");
    if (TEMPORARY.has(err.code)) return verdict("retry", "dns-temporary-failure");
    if (err.code !== "ENODATA") throw err; // something we didn't plan for: surface it
  }

  // RFC 7505: a single MX with preference 0 and exchange "." means "no mail here".
  const isNullMx = (r) => r.priority === 0 && (r.exchange === "" || r.exchange === ".");
  if (mx.length === 1 && isNullMx(mx[0])) return verdict("reject", "null-mx");

  if (mx.length > 0) {
    const hosts = mx.sort((a, b) => a.priority - b.priority).map((r) => r.exchange);
    return verdict("accept", "has-mx", { hosts });
  }

  // RFC 5321 5.1: no MX records -> treat the domain itself as an implicit MX.
  for (const lookup of ["resolve4", "resolve6"]) {
    try {
      const addrs = await resolver[lookup](domain);
      if (addrs.length) return verdict("accept", "implicit-mx", { hosts: [domain] });
    } catch (err) {
      if (TEMPORARY.has(err.code)) return verdict("retry", "dns-temporary-failure");
    }
  }
  return verdict("reject", "no-mail-host");
}

The resolver is injectable, which makes it easy to test without the network. Here's what it returns against a mocked set of zones (run with Node 22):

{"address":"ana@good.test","status":"accept","reason":"has-mx","hosts":["mx1.good.test","mx2.good.test"]}
{"address":"x@nullmx.test","status":"reject","reason":"null-mx"}
{"address":"x@aonly.test","status":"accept","reason":"implicit-mx","hosts":["aonly.test"]}
{"address":"x@nothing.test","status":"reject","reason":"no-mail-host"}
{"address":"x@slow.test","status":"retry","reason":"dns-temporary-failure"}
{"address":"x@typo-domain.test","status":"reject","reason":"domain-does-not-exist"}
{"address":"not-an-email","status":"reject","reason":"bad-syntax"}

Three outcomes, not two. That middle one, retry, is the one most validators get wrong.

Wiring it into a signup form

  • reject: show an inline message ("We can't deliver to that domain. Typo?"). Don't block silently; people fix typos when you tell them.
  • retry: accept the signup, flag the address, and re-check before your first send. A flaky resolver at 2 a.m. should not cost you a customer.
  • accept: send your double opt-in or welcome email. A bounce from that first message is your mailbox-level answer.

Cache results per domain for a few minutes. Your form will see gmail.com thousands of times; DNS doesn't need to.

Common mistakes

  • Rejecting on a timeout. RFC 5321 says temporary errors are retried, not reported as failures. Your validator should agree.
  • Requiring an MX record. The implicit-MX rule means A-record-only domains are legal mail destinations. Rare, but real.
  • Treating null MX as "missing MX". A null MX is a deliberate "no", so it's a hard reject, not a fallback to A records.
  • SMTP-probing from production. It's slow, unreliable against catch-all servers, and can hurt the reputation of the IP you send real mail from.
  • Over-strict regexes. + tags, subdomains and long TLDs are all valid. Keep syntax checks loose and let DNS do the real work.

Checklist

  • [ ] Loose syntax check, length limits from RFC 5321
  • [ ] MX lookup, with ENOTFOUND as reject and timeouts as retry
  • [ ] Null MX (RFC 7505) as a hard reject
  • [ ] A/AAAA fallback for the implicit MX
  • [ ] Per-domain caching
  • [ ] Double opt-in for mailbox-level proof

Want to eyeball a domain by hand first? Our free MX lookup tool shows the records this code reads. And if you're sending receipts and resets from your app, Email Digit's transactional email API for developers checks suppression on every send, so an address that already bounced doesn't get a second chance to hurt you.

FAQ

Is a DNS check enough to verify an email address?
No. It proves the domain can receive mail, not that the mailbox exists. Pair it with a confirmation email.

Should I reject signups when the DNS lookup times out?
No. Treat it as "retry": accept, flag, and re-check before the first send.

What does a null MX record look like?
A single MX with preference 0 and . as the host (RFC 7505). It means the domain accepts no mail.

I work on Email Digit. Drafted with AI assistance and checked against RFC 5321 and RFC 7505.

articles.title: A Browser Dashboard for a ROS 2 Sensor Rig
articles.description: A Vue dashboard for a ROS 2 sensor rig at SMLab, NISER: rosbridge, compressed camera streams, rosbag recording and playback, and a browser terminal.
articles.body_html:
Originally published at aharshit123456.space.

From May to October 2024 I was a research intern at SMLab, NISER, on Swayansaasita, the lab's project to collect a multimodal driving dataset for autonomous two-wheelers. The sensors ran on Jetson boards under ROS 2, and bringing them up, checking every stream and starting a recording all meant SSH sessions and terminal commands. My job was a web page that did those things: start the sensors, show which topics were publishing and how fast, start and stop a recording, show disk space, list past recordings, and preview a stream. This post explains how it works, from rosbridge and compressed images to the two backends I wrote, and which parts were still placeholders when I stopped.

  • 12 of 13 commits in the lab's dashboard repo are mine
  • 114 topics in one ros2 topic list capture from the rig
  • 14.7 MB one ZED point cloud message, before base64
  • 2 backends: Express over SSH, then FastAPI on the rig

Note: Sources: the lab's dashboard repo (Vue app, Express server, FastAPI server; commits from 12 June to 25 August 2024), my earlier ros-webinterface repo (29 May), a small Vue prototype (11 June), and my work notes from the internship. Network addresses, usernames and passwords in the code are left out of every excerpt.

The rig and what it publishes

I didn't build the rig, so I'll describe it only as far as the code shows. The launch script started drivers for a ZED stereo camera, a CS20 time-of-flight depth camera (the kill endpoint matches its processes as synexens), a u-blox GPS receiver (matched as ublox), plus a topic-rate monitor, a disk monitor and rosbridge. Topic names carry the board and camera, such as /Jetson1/camera1/zed_node/imu/data, and my June notes describe calling the recording service "in both the nodes (jetsons)".

On 27 May I saved the output of ros2 topic list and a few ros2 topic echo dumps into the first repo so I could design against real messages. That one capture had 114 topics, 95 of them from the ZED wrapper:

What it is Example topic ROS message type What the dashboard did with it
Rectified colour image /zed/zed_node/left/image_rect_color sensor_msgs/Image Too big to send raw (see below)
Same image, JPEG .../image_rect_color/compressed sensor_msgs/CompressedImage Shown in an <img> tag
Point cloud /zed/zed_node/point_cloud/cloud_registered sensor_msgs/PointCloud2 Decoded, never rendered
IMU /zed/zed_node/imu/data sensor_msgs/Imu Live D3 line charts
Pose, odometry /zed/zed_node/pose, /zed/zed_node/odom geometry_msgs/PoseStamped, nav_msgs/Odometry Not used
Depth and IR (depth camera) /camera1/depth_raw, /camera1/ir_raw sensor_msgs/Image IR JPEG used as the image preview

ROS 2 in a few paragraphs

If you haven't used ROS, here is the vocabulary the rest of this post needs.

  • A node is a process that does one job: a camera driver, a GPS driver, a recorder.
  • A topic is a named channel. Nodes publish messages to a topic and other nodes subscribe to it. Publishers don't know who is listening. /zed/zed_node/imu/data is a topic.
  • A message is a typed struct defined in a .msg file. sensor_msgs/Imu has an orientation quaternion, an angular velocity, a linear acceleration and covariance matrices. Every sensor message starts with a header holding a timestamp and a coordinate frame name.
  • A service is request and response, like a function call between nodes. std_srvs/Trigger takes no arguments and returns success (a bool) and message (a string). The rig's start and stop recording were Trigger services.
  • A launch file starts a set of nodes with their parameters in one command (ros2 launch <package> <file>).
  • A bag is a recording: ros2 bag record writes every message on chosen topics, with timestamps, to disk, and ros2 bag play republishes them later as if the sensors were live.
  • The ZED camera also has its own recording format, SVO, which stores the stereo video and the camera's sensor data and can be replayed through the ZED SDK. The rig recorded both bags and SVO files.

One more ROS tool matters here: image_transport. A camera driver that uses it publishes each image topic several times: raw, /compressed (JPEG or PNG), /compressedDepth (PNG for depth images) and /theora (a video codec). In my capture, 17 topics each had those three suffixes. So I could choose an encoding without touching the drivers.

Why a browser

My notes list three goals for the interface: show left and right camera, point cloud, GPS and IMU data; keep latency minimal with a live feed; and give control over the rig. A web page fits that: any laptop on the lab network can open it with nothing installed, and buttons replace commands that otherwise get typed from memory in a terminal.

Getting ROS into a browser: rosbridge

A browser can't join a ROS 2 network directly. rosbridge is a ROS node that runs a WebSocket server (port 9090 by default) and translates between ROS and JSON. The browser sends {"op": "subscribe", "topic": "/imu", "type": "sensor_msgs/msg/Imu"}; rosbridge subscribes on its behalf and forwards every message as {"op": "publish", "topic": ..., "msg": {...}}. Service calls go the same way with call_service. roslibjs is the JavaScript client that wraps that protocol in Ros, Topic and Service objects.

Sensor drivers on the Jetsons → ROS 2 topics and services → rosbridge ROS ↔ JSON over WebSocket → roslibjs in the browser

Fig. 1 — the data path for everything the dashboard reads. Binary fields such as image bytes arrive as base64 strings inside the JSON.

The detail that shaped every decision later: rosbridge sends uint8[] fields, which is where images and point clouds keep their bytes, as base64 text inside JSON. Base64 makes data a third bigger, and the browser then has to parse it on the main thread.

Version one: one HTML page per sensor (May)

The first repo, ros-webinterface, is plain HTML. index.html stacks three iframes in 16:9 boxes, one per sensor page, and each page opens its own rosbridge connection.

Images took three attempts. My notes from 27 May record them:

  1. Raw sensor_msgs/Image. My notes say each message was about 5 MB, and I dropped it. That fits the arithmetic if the camera ran at the same 1280×720 as its point cloud: a 720p frame in 4-byte BGRA is 3.7 MB, and base64 makes it about 4.9 MB, per frame, per viewer. A web worker that swaps BGR to RGBA for a <canvas> is still in the repo from that attempt.
  2. Theora video through ogv.js, a JavaScript video decoder. I couldn't get its decoder object to initialise.
  3. CompressedImage (JPEG). At first I couldn't find a library to decode it. The next day I realised I didn't need one: the browser already decodes JPEG, and the base64 string rosbridge sends is exactly what a data: URL wants. 
const listener = new ROSLIB.Topic({
  ros,
  name: "/zed/zed_node/stereo_raw/image_raw_color/compressed",
  messageType: "sensor_msgs/msg/CompressedImage",
});

listener.subscribe((message) => {
  // message.data is already base64 JPEG bytes
  document.getElementById("imageDisplay")
    .setAttribute("src", "data:image/jpeg;base64," + message.data);
});

That became the image preview for the rest of the project.

The IMU page draws linear_acceleration with D3, keeping a sliding one-second window. The first version had a copy-paste bug: the third chart, meant for z, plotted y a second time. The later version fixes it and averages samples into 50 ms bins before drawing, so each redraw plots about 20 averaged points for the one-second window instead of every raw sample.

The point cloud page set up a Three.js scene with orbit controls and subscribed to a PointCloud2 topic, but its convertPointCloud2ToVertices function returned an empty array. The parsing was the hard part, and it wasn't written yet.

The same day I scaffolded an Angular app around those pages and left it there; my July report says I tried React, Angular and Next before choosing Vue with Vite.

Latency and size

The table below is the reasoning I wish I had written down at the start. Sizes come from the message dumps I saved on 27 May.

Stream One message on the wire Decision
Raw colour image About 5 MB (my notes) Dropped
JPEG CompressedImage Far smaller; varies with the scene Used: data: URL, browser decodes
Theora video Not measured Dropped: decoder wouldn't initialise
ZED point cloud, 1280×720, 16 bytes per point 14.7 MB raw, ~19.7 MB as base64 Decoded only, never drawn
IMU Small: a header, three vectors, three covariance matrices Charted, averaged into 50 ms bins

The point cloud row explains most of the trouble. The ZED wrapper publishes one point per pixel: 921,600 points with four float32 fields each (x, y, z and colour packed into a float), so a single message is 14.7 MB before rosbridge turns it into text. No browser tab keeps up with that at camera rate. The real fixes are upstream: publish a downsampled cloud, lower the wrapper's point cloud rate, or decode in a worker from a binary transport. My notes mark "configure the PointCloud streaming and make it lighter weight" as done in late June, but that change lived in the rig's configuration, not in either repo, so I can't show what it was.

Two other ideas never reached these repos: a server-side compression step between rosbridge and the browser (2 June), and streaming ZED frames from the ZED SDK directly, outside ROS. For the second, the README logs my changes to the SDK's SVO recording sample on the rig to turn on its streaming mode; my July report marks it "integration pending".

The Vue app (June to August)

The dashboard proper is a Vue 3 app built with Vite, in the lab's repo. I made 12 of its 13 commits; the remaining one is the lab account's initial commit. The final screen has a header row of buttons (Start ROS, Reboot System, Kill System, Start Frequency), a table of topics in the middle, and a black footer with the recording controls, disk usage and the current file.

Browser Vue app → rosbridge WebSocket topics + record services → ROS 2 on the rig

Browser Vue app → Local API server :3000 start, kill, reboot, logs → SSH, later a child process

Fig. 2 — two paths. ROS data and recording go through rosbridge. Anything rosbridge can't do, such as launching ROS itself, goes through a small HTTP server.

The second path exists because of a chicken-and-egg problem: rosbridge is one of the things the launch file starts, so the browser can't use rosbridge to start ROS. Process control needs something outside ROS.

Topic health: the frequency table

The rig ran a monitor node that published every topic's rate as one JSON string on /topic_status. The browser subscribes once and fills a reactive dictionary that the table renders:

const frequencyTopic = new ROSLIB.Topic({
  ros, name: '/topic_status', messageType: 'std_msgs/msg/String'
});

frequencyTopic.subscribe(message => {
  const data = JSON.parse(message.data);   // { "/topic": hz, ... }
  for (let topic in data) {
    if (!topicFrequencyDict[topic]) topicFrequencyDict[topic] = { frequency: data[topic] };
    else topicFrequencyDict[topic].frequency = data[topic];
  }
});

JSON inside a std_msgs/String is a shortcut, but a useful one: a custom message type would have to be defined, built and installed on every machine that touches it, while a string works everywhere. Each row shows the topic, its rate, Active or Inactive, and a Preview/Debug button. This table is the part I'd keep unchanged: one glance tells you whether every sensor is up before you press record.

Start, kill and reboot

The first backend was an Express server using the ssh2 library. Start ROS opened an SSH session to the Jetson and ran bash start_ros.sh. Kill System ran kill_ros.sh. Reboot ran sudo reboot. The README warns users to refresh the page after Start ROS, and the code does window.location.reload() itself. The reason is that the page opens its rosbridge connection when it loads, which is before rosbridge exists, and roslibjs doesn't reconnect on its own.

Recording

The 11 June prototype called the ZED wrapper's own SVO service directly, with a fixed filename and an automatic stop:

const service = new ROSLIB.Service({
  ros, name: '/Jetson1/camera1/zed_node/start_svo_rec',
  serviceType: 'zed_interfaces/srv/StartSvoRec'
});
service.callService(new ROSLIB.ServiceRequest({ svo_filename: 'file5.svo' }), ...);
setTimeout(() => { /* call stop_svo_rec */ }, 5000);

By late July the rig had /start_recording and /stop_recording services of type std_srvs/Trigger. The recorder node behind them isn't in this repo. It returned the session's path in the message field, which the dashboard displays as the file name. On success the button turns red and disabled and a one-second timer starts:

service.callService(request, result => {
  if (result.success) {
    const startTime = Date.now();
    timerInterval = setInterval(() => {
      elapsedTime = Math.floor((Date.now() - startTime) / 1000);
    }, 1000);
    fileName = result.message;      // e.g. ".../CS2303DATA/CS2303-019"
    getFileSize(fileName);
  }
});

Fig. 3 — the console during a test recording on 31 July, with the home directory blacked out. The session path comes back in the Trigger response. File size is a placeholder, and the stop service answered twice.

That screenshot is from the day I wrote "seems to be working fine I guess" in my notes, and it shows what wasn't:

  • File size was static. getFileSize exists, but its own comment says "TODO Currently of no use". Size was never polled while recording.
  • The footer didn't update by itself. fileName, fileSize and elapsedTime are plain variables, not Vue refs, so the template only shows new values when something else triggers a re-render, such as the next frequency update. The console shows the timer working; the screen didn't reliably show it.
  • Stop was glitchy. My notes list it as high priority with "sometimes not working", and the screenshot ends with two stop responses for one session. Making the button wait until the file was actually closed needed the recorder to report it, which was server-side.
  • My notes also mark "only enable start recording if all topic frequencies are non-zero" as done, but I can't find that check in the committed code.

The playback list

Each session was appended to a log.csv on the rig: session id, date, start time, stop time, duration and file size. The server reads it and returns JSON. (The header in the data really is spelled Sesion-id, so the Vue code has to spell it that way too.) Playback Recordings shows the rows in a table with a Play button on each.

Play is where the browser part stops. It opens a GridLayout component meant to show the session's streams in movable panes; it renders three hard-coded tiles labelled "Item 1" to "Item 3". My notes say I wrote rosbag and SVO playback scripts for the rig, but they aren't in this repo and the browser was never connected to them.

The disk monitor

A disk monitor node published df output as JSON on /disk_space. df reports Used and 1K-blocks in kibibytes, so dividing by 1024² gives GiB, and the footer shows used over total. Two cosmetic bugs survived: before the first message arrives it shows NaN GB, and the template appends "GB" twice ("... GB / ... GB GB Used"). Disk space matters on a recording rig: sensor sessions are large, and running out mid-ride loses the session.

The preview button

This feature changed the most. On 25 June I tried a batch preview: an inline D3 chart or canvas inside every topic tile, fed by IMU samples pushed into a reactive array that every tile watched. The commit is honestly titled "batch preview feature failed to integrate", and it also checked in a Chrome performance trace from that afternoon. The next two days I switched to a popup per topic: the button opens a window and adds an iframe for the right viewer, with a close button underneath.

const deviceType = topic.toLowerCase();
if (deviceType.includes('point'))      iframe.src = "../src/assets/pointcloud3.html";
else if (deviceType.includes('raw'))   iframe.src = "../src/assets/home.html";
else if (deviceType.includes('imu'))   iframe.src = "../src/assets/graph.html";
else if (deviceType.includes('fix'))   iframe.src = "../src/assets/map.html";
else { window.alert(`Invalid Topic`); return; }

Moving each viewer into its own iframe gave every stream its own connection and its own page lifecycle: closing the iframe ends its subscription, so a forgotten preview can't keep pulling a heavy topic. That was the point of the "linear lifecycle" commit.

The honest state of the viewers at the end:

  • The image viewer works, but it always subscribes to one hard-coded IR image topic from the depth camera, whichever image topic you clicked.
  • The IMU charts work, with a leak: the sample arrays only ever grow, and every new message filters the whole history, so a preview left open slows down over time.
  • The point cloud viewer decodes x, y and z from the base64 buffer (16-byte stride, three float32 offsets) and logs them to the console. It draws nothing. My July report says a Three.js version worked; the committed file isn't that version.
  • The GPS map is a stub page with a heading. It reads topic and type from its URL query, which shows the plan: pass the clicked topic into the viewer. The line in the app that would do that is commented out.

FireAPI: moving the backend onto the rig

In August I wrote a second backend, API_server.py. The commit calls it "FireAPI"; it is a FastAPI app with the same endpoints as the Express server (/start-ros, /kill-ros, /reboot-system, /log-file, /get-file-size) plus /stop-ros, /ros-status and a WebSocket at /ws/logs. Because the paths match, the Vue app didn't need to change. The main difference is where it runs: on the ROS machine itself, starting the launch file as a child process instead of over SSH.

@app.post("/start-ros")
async def start_ros():
    if ros_process["process"] is not None:
        return {"message": "ROS2 launch file is already running", ...}
    process = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
        'ros2', 'launch', 'daemon', 'init.launch.py',
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE
    )
    ros_process["process"] = process
    ...
Express + ssh2 (June) FastAPI (August)
Runs on Wherever it's started; reaches the Jetson over SSH The ROS machine
Starts ROS bash start_ros.sh over SSH ros2 launch as a child process it keeps a handle to
Knows if ROS is running No Stores the process; refuses a second start
Credentials Hard-coded SSH password in source None needed
Shell commands du -sh ${fileName} built as a string: command injection Argument lists, no shell
Live logs No /ws/logs streams the launch's output

It was a clear improvement, and re-reading it now I can see four problems:

  • /ros-status crashes. It calls .poll(), which exists on subprocess.Popen but not on the asyncio process object, so the endpoint raises an error.
  • /kill-ros is very broad. It runs ros2 daemon stop, pkill -f ros2, kills the driver processes and rosbridge, then, if ps aux still mentions "ros" anywhere, runs pkill -f ros, which matches any process whose command line contains those three letters.
  • Undrained pipes can stall ROS. stderr is piped and never read, and stdout is read only while the log terminal is open. Once a pipe's buffer fills, the launch process blocks on its next write.
  • No authentication, and CORS allows any origin, on endpoints that reboot the machine. Acceptable on an isolated lab network, risky anywhere else.

A terminal in the browser

The last feature was the in-browser terminal: an xterm.js terminal, sized with its fit addon, inside a modal. Opening it connects to /ws/logs and writes whatever arrives:

socket.value = new WebSocket('ws://localhost:3000/ws/logs');
socket.value.onmessage = async (event) => {
  terminal.write(event.data instanceof Blob ? await event.data.text() : event.data);
};

On the server, the WebSocket handler reads the launch process's stdout line by line and forwards each line. So it's a read-only log viewer, not a shell: nothing typed goes back to the machine. For seeing why a driver failed to start, that's the right scope; a real shell on an unauthenticated server would be a remote-access hole.

What was unfinished

By the last commit in August, these were the gaps:

  • Playback in the browser: the grid is a placeholder.
  • Point cloud and GPS previews: decode-only and stub.
  • Per-topic previews: viewers are chosen by substring and subscribe to hard-coded topics.
  • Live file size during a recording, and a stop button that waits for the recorder.
  • Start recording gated on every topic being live: in my notes, not in the code.
  • Reconnection: refreshing the page was the reconnect strategy.
  • Hard-coded addresses and credentials in the Express server and the HTML viewers.

What I'd do differently

  • One rosbridge connection with reconnection and a status banner, instead of one per iframe and a page refresh.
  • Throttle at the source. roslibjs can ask rosbridge for a throttle_rate, and a preview needs a few frames per second, not thirty. For point clouds, a downsampled preview topic on the rig.
  • Pass the topic and message type to every viewer and make them generic: one image viewer for any CompressedImage topic, one chart for any Imu.
  • Let the recorder own state. Publish a recording-status topic (file, size, duration, closed or not) and have the UI only display it.
  • Look at existing tools first. My earliest page was built from Foxglove's rosbridge tutorial. Before writing viewers by hand again, I'd check how far an existing robotics visualiser gets, and build only the rig-specific controls.

The lesson that stuck: the hard parts weren't Vue or D3. They were bytes (what one message costs once it becomes JSON) and state (who knows whether ROS is running, or whether a recording really stopped). Both are easier to get right on the robot side than in the browser.

More from Research at NISER & IISER Bhopal

  • NISER Internship Retrospective: going back to the lab, and what the internship gave me.
  • From ORB Features to ORB-SLAM3: the lab talk on feature extraction, matching and ORB-SLAM3.
  • SLAM from the Bayes Filter Up: the probabilistic basics behind SLAM.
  • Turning an iPhone into a LiDAR, IMU and GPS Sensor: streaming phone sensors over TCP, and an ARKit scanner that exports meshes.
  • Field Notes on Perception for Two-Wheeler Autonomy: computer vision, point clouds and prediction for autonomous two-wheelers, written for the Swayansaasita project site.
  • Hands-on Quantum Programming at IISER Bhopal: qubits, Bell states and Deutsch–Jozsa worked through from scratch at the QuCIS workshop.

articles.title: Before Switching to P2P, I Measured Whether WebRTC Would Even Connect
articles.description: I'm building Clipboard Share, a browser clipboard for moving files between devices on the same...
articles.body_html:
I'm building Clipboard Share, a browser clipboard for moving files between devices on the same network: https://www.clipboardapp.org. I wanted to make transfers faster by using WebRTC. Before changing anything, I shipped a small probe that only measures whether a direct connection works.

One thing up front: file transfer is still not P2P. Files go to Cloudflare R2 and the receiver downloads from R2. The only place in the codebase that creates a DataChannel is the probe, and it sends throwaway test data.

Why I looked at P2P

The current flow is "upload everything, then download." With a multi-GB file, the receiver waits for the whole upload even if the sender is sitting next to them. The goal in docs/p2p-decision.md:

When the other device is already in the room, send the file over WebRTC directly and cut the wait of "download only after the upload finishes."

Why measure first

Direct connections fail in some network setups, and a device that joins later can't receive anything over a connection that no longer exists. So the doc states a rule before any data came in:

Files are always stored in R2. P2P is only a faster path for devices that were already connected at send time. Devices that join later, or refresh, get the file from R2 as they do today.

It also fixes the pass criteria up front (dated 2026-10-24): C1 connection rate >= 85%, C2 transfer completion >= 97% with zero mismatches, C3 P2P median speed bucket at least one step above R2 uploads, C4 at least 30 uploads of 8 MB+ in 7 days. Miss any one and the next step doesn't happen. If it passes, the next step is a "shadow mode": keep uploading to R2 as usual, and have the receiver verify P2P data with SHA-256 per 1 MB, then discard it.

How the probe works

Nothing changes on screen. When a device joins a room that already has another device, it tries to connect and reports the result as a GA4 p2p_probe event.

1. The server only relays signaling

Offers, answers and ICE candidates travel over a Socket.IO event, p2p:signal. The handler forwards {to, data} as {from, data}, and only to a socket in the same IP room:

const ipRoomId = socket.ipRoomId;
if (!ipRoomId || to === socket.id) return;
const target = io.sockets.sockets.get(to) as ExtendedSocket | undefined;
if (!target || target.ipRoomId !== ipRoomId || !target.rooms.has(ipRoomId)) return;

target.emit('p2p:signal', { from: socket.id, data });

The only thing it checks about data is its size (16 KB cap after JSON serialization). There's also a per-socket token bucket (burst 40, 20/sec).

2. Classify how it connected

Once the channel opens, I read the selected candidate pair from getStats(). There's no TURN server, so a relay candidate counts as a failure.

export function classifyCandidateTypes(localType, remoteType) {
  const valid = ['host', 'srflx', 'prflx', 'relay']
  if (!valid.includes(localType) || !valid.includes(remoteType)) return 'failed'
  if (localType === 'relay' || remoteType === 'relay') return 'failed'
  if (localType === 'srflx' || remoteType === 'srflx') return 'direct_nat'
  return 'direct_lan' // host/prflx
}

3. Send test data and verify it

A connected channel can still be useless, so the probe actually sends data: 8 MB on a LAN path, 2 MB through NAT. Each 16 KB chunk starts with its index; the receiver only counts bytes and checks order, then drops the data.

export const PROBE_BYTES_LAN = 8 * 1024 * 1024
export const PROBE_BYTES_NAT = 2 * 1024 * 1024

// receiver: replies ack:<bytes>:<ok|bad> on the end signal
recvBytes += d?.byteLength ?? 0
if (readChunkIndex(d) !== expectIdx) orderOk = false
expectIdx++

The sender marks it complete only if the acked byte count matches and the order flag is ok; otherwise mismatch. The transfer timeout scales with size: max(8 s, bytes / 1.5 Mbit/s), capped at 30 s. If the connection itself isn't up in 8 seconds, it's failed.

4. Once per session, and it can't break the app 

export const SESSION_FLAG = 'p2p_probe_done'

export function isProbeEnabled(envValue = import.meta.env?.VITE_P2P_PROBE_ENABLED) {
  return envValue !== 'false'
}

One probe per session (sessionStorage), every exception is swallowed with a console.warn, and VITE_P2P_PROBE_ENABLED=false turns it off. The unit tests cover timeout to failed, mismatch on bad bytes or order, stalled when no ack arrives, and closed when the channel drops mid-transfer.

For comparison I also log real R2 upload speed: a successful upload of 8 MB or more sends an upload_perf event (upload_mbps, upload_path, retries, resumed, and so on). P2P only matters if it beats that.

Results

Between Oct 24 and Nov 25, GA4 recorded 672 p2p_probe events from 428 users. 177 of them came in the last 7 days, so the probe is still running.

What Count
Probes that got an answer from the peer (got_answer=true) 533
Direct connection direct_lan / direct_nat 394 / 39
Connection failed 238
Test transfer complete / stalled / other (closed, error, complete_legacy) 395 / 30 / 3
Data mismatch 0

Checked against the thresholds I wrote down first:

  • C1 connection rate: 433 direct ÷ 533 answered ≈ 81%. Below the 85% bar.
  • C2 transfer completion: 395 complete out of 428 test transfers ≈ 92%. Below the 97% bar. There were zero mismatches, so data never arrived wrong; most of the gap is stalled (no reply to the end signal).
  • C3 speed and C4 demand: the upload_perf event I use as the R2 baseline shows 0 events in GA4 for this period. I haven't found out why yet, so I can't judge speed or demand.

The rule was "if any check misses, don't move to the next step." With these numbers, shadow mode doesn't start.

What's still weak

  • One probe per session with 2-8 MB of data. It may not match a multi-GB transfer.
  • Results are GA4 aggregates, so I can't drill into which device pairs fail.
  • It only tries the first peer in the room (peers[0]), so a room with many devices is measured as one pair.
  • STUN only, no TURN. Networks that block direct connections simply count as failures.
  • There is no P2P file transfer code today. The criteria are written down, but the shadow-mode step and anything after it don't exist yet.

I built this with Claude Code. If you try it, I'd like to hear what's rough. There's a feedback link at the bottom of the site: https://www.clipboardapp.org

Originally published in Korean on velog.

articles.title: How I Built a 200-Page Red/Blue PDF Blueprint Overlay & Diff Tool 100% in Browser Canvas (Zero Backend)
articles.description: Every week, construction estimators and paralegals run into the same frustrating problem: an...
articles.body_html:
Every week, construction estimators and paralegals run into the same frustrating problem: an architect drops Addendum 4 (200+ pages) forty-eight hours before bid day, or opposing counsel sends back a revised PDF contract.

The existing options all have painful tradeoffs:

Enterprise suites like Bluebeam Revu moved to expensive annual per-seat subscriptions.
Free online PDF diff websites require uploading confidential bid sets or legal contracts to someone else's server.
Most desktop perpetual tools are Windows-only and blocked in locked-down corporate browser environments.

I wanted to see if a modern browser (Chrome, Edge, or Safari) could handle both 200-page text diffs and Bluebeam-style Red/Blue pixel overlays strictly inside local RAM — with zero backend servers and zero file uploads.

Here is the architecture behind RedlineZero and the three tricky engineering problems I had to solve.

  1. Reconstructing Readable Lines from pdfjs-dist (Not Raw Stream Order)

If you naively join page.getTextContent().items, PDFs often store text fragments out of visual order (headers, footers, and table columns jump around).

To make line-by-line diffs readable, I bucket TextItems by their PDF Y-coordinate (with a 3.5pt tolerance) and sort each horizontal row by X-coordinate:

ts
tokens.sort((a, b) => {
if (Math.abs(a.y - b.y) > 3.5) return b.y - a.y; // top-to-bottom
return a.x - b.x; // left-to-right
});

  1. Bounded LCS + Inline Word/Number Highlighting Without Freezing the Tab

When comparing a 200-page addendum, two things can kill UX:

Main-thread freezes: Extracting and diffing 200 pages synchronously locks the browser. Yielding every 4 pages (await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))) keeps a live progress bar silky smooth.
Whole-line highlights hide the actual change: Estimators don't want to scan two 30-word sentences to see what changed — they want to see 4,000 → 5,000 or $12,000 → $18,500 pop out in 0.2 seconds.

By trimming common prefixes/suffixes before running a Uint16Array LCS table (with a memory guard for gigantic pages) and then pairing adjacent remove + add lines for a secondary token-level diff, changed numbers and clauses light up immediately.

  1. Classic Red/Blue Pixel Blueprint Overlay in HTML5 Canvas

Text diffs are useless when an architect moves a partition wall or adds an HVAC diffuser on a vector/scanned floor plan.

For visual comparison, I render Page A and Page B onto two white-padded offscreen canvases (supporting an X/Y pixel alignment nudge for slightly shifted scans) and compute per-pixel luminance:

ts
const lumOld = 0.299 * dataOld[i] + 0.587 * dataOld[i + 1] + 0.114 * dataOld[i + 2];
const lumNew = 0.299 * dataNew[i] + 0.587 * dataNew[i + 1] + 0.114 * dataNew[i + 2];
if (Math.abs(lumOld - lumNew) <= threshold) {
// Unchanged ink fades to neutral gray so revisions pop
const avg = (lumOld + lumNew) * 0.5;
const faded = avg > 245 ? 255 : Math.min(245, Math.round(avg + (255 - avg) * 0.42));
out[i] = out[i + 1] = out[i + 2] = faded;
} else if (lumOld < lumNew) {
// Darker in Original => Removed => Vivid Red
out[i] = 220; out[i + 1] = 38; out[i + 2] = 38;
} else {
// Darker in Revised => Added => Vivid Blue
out[i] = 37; out[i + 1] = 99; out[i + 2] = 235;
}

Unchanged walls and gridlines fade softly to gray, deleted geometry turns crisp Red, and new additions turn Blue — with an instant Side-by-Side / Doc A / Doc B toggle right in the toolbar whenever overlapping text needs to be read clearly.

Try It Offline (No Signup Required)

You can test the full workflow right now with the built-in 3-page sample construction addendum (or your own PDFs — free up to 5 pages, zero uploads, works even if you disconnect your Wi-Fi after loading):

👉 https://diff.tensorvisualworks.com/

I'd love feedback from anyone who deals with large PDF revisions or scanned drawings — what edge cases break your current workflow?

articles.title: How to Generate Crisp Procedural Pixel-Art Explosions, Sword Slashes & Godot 4 SpriteFrames (.tres) in Pure JS
articles.description: Most browser-based particle generators have the same giveaway: blurry, semi-transparent soft circles...
articles.body_html:
Most browser-based particle generators have the same giveaway: blurry, semi-transparent soft circles that immediately clash with hand-drawn 2D pixel art.

While building PixelBurst 2D v1.5 (a zero-dependency browser studio for procedural pixel explosions, sword slashes, laser beams, bouncing debris, and lightning sprite sheets), I found that getting authentic Metal Slug / Dead Cells / Celeste-style pixel VFX comes down to three surprisingly compact rendering techniques — plus eliminating the tedious manual slicing step in Godot 4.

Here is the exact pipeline, complete with copy-pasteable code.

1. Ditch Alpha Blending — Render to a Scalar Heat/Density Field + Bayer 4×4 Dither

Instead of drawing anti-aliased radial gradients directly to a 2D <canvas>, simulate particles into two integer-resolution Float32Array buffers (64×64):

  • density[x + y * W]: accumulated particle / shockwave / slash mass
  • heat[x + y * W]: maximum temperature (0.0 cool smoke → 1.0 white-hot core)

When quantizing those buffers into RGBA pixels, apply a hard alpha threshold (every pixel is strictly alpha = 0 or alpha = 255) combined with a 4×4 Bayer ordered dithering matrix mapped onto a curated 5-stop color ramp:

const BAYER4 = [
   0/16 - 0.5,  8/16 - 0.5,  2/16 - 0.5, 10/16 - 0.5,
  12/16 - 0.5,  4/16 - 0.5, 14/16 - 0.5,  6/16 - 0.5,
   3/16 - 0.5, 11/16 - 0.5,  1/16 - 0.5,  9/16 - 0.5,
  15/16 - 0.5,  7/16 - 0.5, 13/16 - 0.5,  5/16 - 0.5
];

// Quantize density & heat into crisp 5-color pixel art
for (let y = 0; y < h; y++) {
  const bayerRow = (y & 3) * 4;
  for (let x = 0; x < w; x++) {
    const idx = y * w + x;
    const bayer = BAYER4[bayerRow + (x & 3)];
    const cut = threshold + bayer * ditherAmount * 0.22;
    if (density[idx] < cut) continue; // 100% transparent

    mask[idx] = 1; // opaque silhouette
    const hVal = Math.max(0, Math.min(0.999, heat[idx] * 0.85 + bayer * ditherAmount * 0.24));
    const stopIdx = Math.floor((1 - hVal) * paletteStops.length);
    const [r, g, b] = paletteStops[stopIdx];
    const p4 = idx * 4;
    rgba[p4] = r; rgba[p4 + 1] = g; rgba[p4 + 2] = b; rgba[p4 + 3] = 255;
  }
}

Adding a subtle coherent 2D value-noise wobble to density[idx] right before thresholding turns round blobs into organic billowing pixel fireballs and smoke clouds.

2. The 1px Pixel-Art Outline Pass (Instant Studio Polish)

Once mask[] holds your crisp binary silhouette, a single 4-connected neighbor pass wraps every explosion puff, sword slash crescent, and flying spark in a 1px dark (or bright rim) pixel outline:

for (let y = 0; y < h; y++) {
  for (let x = 0; x < w; x++) {
    const idx = y * w + x;
    if (mask[idx] !== 0) continue;
    const touchesSprite =
      (y > 0 && mask[idx - w] === 1) ||
      (y < h - 1 && mask[idx + w] === 1) ||
      (x > 0 && mask[idx - 1] === 1) ||
      (x < w - 1 && mask[idx + 1] === 1);

    if (touchesSprite) {
      const p4 = idx * 4;
      rgba[p4] = outlineRgb[0];
      rgba[p4 + 1] = outlineRgb[1];
      rgba[p4 + 2] = outlineRgb[2];
      rgba[p4 + 3] = 255;
    }
  }
}

Also watch out for Frame 0 input lag: for one-shot combat VFX (hit sparks, sword slashes, muzzle flashes), sample normalized lifetime at (frameIndex + 0.45) / (frameCount + 0.15) instead of frameIndex / (frameCount - 1) so Frame 1 immediately pops with an impact flash instead of sitting blank for 66ms!

3. Auto-Generating Godot 4 SpriteFrames (.tres) Directly in the Browser

Exporting a horizontal PNG strip is only half the workflow — manually creating AnimatedSprite2D frames in Godot takes time when you have dozens of hit sparks and spells.

Because Godot 4 .tres files are clean plain-text resources, you can emit a ready-to-drop SpriteFrames right alongside your baked PNG sheet:

[gd_resource type="SpriteFrames" load_steps=16 format=3]

[ext_resource type="Texture2D" path="res://classic_fireball_sheet.png" id="1_sheet"]

[sub_resource type="AtlasTexture" id="AtlasTexture_000"]
atlas = ExtResource("1_sheet")
region = Rect2(0, 0, 64, 64)

[sub_resource type="AtlasTexture" id="AtlasTexture_001"]
atlas = ExtResource("1_sheet")
region = Rect2(64, 0, 64, 64)

[resource]
animations = [{
"frames": [{
"duration": 1.0,
"texture": SubResource("AtlasTexture_000")
}, {
"duration": 1.0,
"texture": SubResource("AtlasTexture_001")
}],
"loop": false,
"name": &"default",
"speed": 15.0
}]

Drop both classic_fireball_sheet.png and classic_fireball_SpriteFrames.tres into res://, assign the .tres to any AnimatedSprite2D, and it plays immediately at exact FPS with crisp nearest-neighbor bounds.

Try the Live Browser Studio (Free Web Demo v1.5)

I packaged this entire engine — expanded in v1.5 to 30 Studio Presets, 9 stackable procedural layer types (Explosions, Shockwave Rings, Sword Slashes, Impact Stars, Vortex/Plumes, Pixel Lightning, Laser Beams, Bouncing Shards/Debris, and Directional Cone Fire Breath), 18 palettes, 2-Way / 4-Way Mirror Symmetry, Onion Skinning, and JSON Recipe Save/Load — into PixelBurst 2D.

  • Offline Pro Edition ($6.99 — Launch Week 35% Off applied via link): Unlocks up to 128×128 / 32-frame sheets, Transparent GIF89a, 1-click Godot 4 .tres + Unity Auto-Slice C# + Atlas JSON ZIPs, and 6× Batch Seed Variation Packs with CC0 commercial rights: https://lorialck.gumroad.com/l/pixelburst-2d/LAUNCH35
  • 2-Tool Indie 2D FX Bundle ($9.99, save 33%): Get both PixelBurst 2D v1.5 Pro and ShaderKnit 2D v1.5 Pro (16 stackable 2D sprite shaders) together: https://lorialck.gumroad.com/l/indie-2d-fx-bundle
